## Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, c. 1780–1870

### Jurisdiction Overview
Billy civil parish sits in the barony of Lower Dunluce (partly Carey), Poor Law Union of Coleraine, County Antrim — centred on the post town of **Bushmills**. After 1922 it became part of Northern Ireland. The parish held Presbyterian, Covenanter, Wesleyan Methodist, Church of Ireland, and Catholic congregations, making it a multi-denomination environment relevant to a Presbyterian family.

---

### Civil Registration (Vital Records)
Government registration of **births and deaths** did not begin until **1864**; Protestant marriages were registered from **1845**, all marriages from 1864. For a family researching a birth around 1825, **there is no civil registration** — church registers are the only primary vital-event source for most of this window. Post-1864 civil records are administered through **GRONI** (General Register Office of Northern Ireland).

---

### Church Records

**Presbyterian** — The parish had a Presbyterian meeting house. Presbyterian registers in Ulster average a start date around **1830**, so a c.1825 baptism may simply not be recorded in any surviving Presbyterian register. The specific congregation (e.g., First Bushmills or another meeting house serving Billy parish) and its exact start date were not confirmed by this survey — verify via PRONI's *Guide to Church Records* before targeting a specific congregation.

**Digitized material found (not name-indexed):** `volume_search` located two full-text-searchable (but 0% name-indexed) FamilySearch volumes for **Ballylinny, Billy parish**:
- Christenings, 1837–1868 (image group 007907410_008_M9VF-SK5, 65 images)
- Marriages, 1837–1864 (image group 007765074_009_M9VX-Q7W, 50 images)

Both are searchable via FamilySearch full-text search but cannot be found through the name index. Neither confirms denomination in the tool output — verify before relying on them.

**Church of Ireland** — Records began in 1536, but two-thirds were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin. Even for a Presbyterian family, the standard strategy is to search surviving Church of Ireland registers, as families often appear in both.

**Catholic** — Billy falls in the Catholic district of Coleraine. Most rural Catholic registers in Ulster did not begin until after Catholic Emancipation (1828). Probably does not help for a c.1825 Presbyterian birth, but useful for situating neighbours.

**Covenanter / Wesleyan Methodist** — Both had meeting houses in the parish; no Billy-specific start dates confirmed by this survey.

**Gap to flag:** Presbyterian and Catholic registers frequently lack burial registers — expect gaps for burials even where baptisms/marriages survive.

---

### Census Records
Pre-1864 Irish census material is a **known gap nationwide**: the 1821–1851 censuses were largely destroyed in 1922. No census coverage was confirmed for Billy parish in this survey. Use **Tithe Applotment Books** and **Griffith's Valuation** (below) as census substitutes.

---

### Land / Tax Records (Census Substitutes)
These are the most important substitutes for a missing census:

- **Tithe Applotment Books** (1820s): A tax paid to the Church of Ireland; names heads of household by townland. Directly overlaps the c.1825 birth window.
- **Griffith's Valuation** (1840s–1860s): A property survey for tax purposes. A browse-only valuation volume for Ballylinny, Billy parish, 1867–1881 (VAL 12B/1/7B, image group 004689599, 76 images) was found — browse-only, not indexed.

---

### School Records
One school volume was found: **Deffrick National School Girls** (image group 008682995_005_M94W-68Y), 1 Apr 1867 – 11 Sep 1933, 50 images, browse-only. This falls after the main target window but could capture daughters of the generation you're researching.

---

### Probate / Court Records
No Billy-specific probate collections were returned by this survey. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki's [Ireland Probate Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Probate_Records) page and the index *Ireland, Indexes to Wills, Probate Administration, Marriage Bonds and Licences, 1591–1866* (available at Ancestry).

---

### Repository Guide

**Physical Repositories**

| Repository | Key Holdings |
|---|---|
| **PRONI**, 2 Titanic Boulevard, Belfast BT3 9HQ | Church registers on microfilm/original for all six Ulster counties including Antrim; their *Guide to Church Records* identifies exactly which congregations existed in Billy parish and where their records are held |
| **Church of Ireland RCB Library**, Braemor Park, Dublin 14 | Church of Ireland parish registers; List of Parish Registers finding aid |
| **National Library of Ireland / National Archives** | Catholic parish register microfilm (registers.nli.ie); wills and probate indexes |

**Online**

| Site | What's there for this area |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Ballylinny christenings 1837–1868 and marriages 1837–1864 (full-text searchable, not name-indexed); Ballylinny Valuation 1867–1881 and Deffrick school records (browse-only). No indexed collections returned for Billy parish. |
| **IrishGenealogy.ie** | Linked from Ireland Church Records Wiki page as an index to Catholic and Church of Ireland registers nationally |
| **NLI registers.nli.ie** | Catholic parish register microfilm, free online |

**Coverage note:** `collections_search` returned **zero indexed FamilySearch collections** for Billy parish, and `catalog_search` also returned zero hits. This is a digitization/cataloguing gap, not evidence records don't exist — the records are most likely at PRONI on microfilm.

---

### Known Record Losses
Two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers nationally were destroyed in the 1922 PRO fire. No tool result confirmed survival or loss of Billy parish's specific registers — check with PRONI and the RCB Library to determine what survives for each congregation.

---

### Practical Next Steps for a c.1825 Presbyterian Birth in Billy Parish

1. **Contact PRONI** (proni@communities-ni.gov.uk) and request their *Guide to Church Records* to identify which Presbyterian meeting house(s) served Billy/Bushmills and whether their registers reach back to the 1820s.
2. **Search the Tithe Applotment Books** (1820s) for the townland(s) where the family lived — will name the father as head of household and confirm presence in the parish around the birth year.
3. **Search the Ballylinny christening volume** (FamilySearch, full-text, 1837–1868) for younger siblings; marriages (1837–1864) for the subject or siblings; both are good for establishing parents' names even if the c.1825 birth itself is too early.
4. **Search Church of Ireland registers** for Billy parish even though the family was Presbyterian — siblings and collateral relatives frequently appear across denominations.
5. **Check Griffith's Valuation** (1840s–1860s) for the family in Billy parish townlands as a secondary census substitute confirming the family's landholding by mid-century.
6. Be prepared for the possibility that **no surviving Presbyterian baptism register reaches 1825** in this parish — in that case, the Tithe Applotment Books and later sources (Griffith's, church marriage records) become the foundation for proving parentage circumstantially.

output.text_response:
# Locality Guide: County Cork, Ireland (1830s–1840s)

## Jurisdiction Overview
County Cork is one of Ireland's historic counties in the province of Munster, with Cork City as its administrative center. The Great Famine began in 1845 at the tail of this period, and the 1922 Four Courts fire later destroyed most pre-1901 Irish census returns — both critically important facts for research in this era.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Bad news:** No civil birth, death, or Catholic marriage records exist for the 1830s–1840s. State civil registration didn't begin until **1 January 1864**; non-Catholic (Church of Ireland) marriages were registered only from 1845.
- **What to use instead:** Church records (see below).

### Church Records
- **Denominations:** Roman Catholic (the majority) and Church of Ireland (Anglican).
- **Record types:** Baptisms and marriages; burials were rarely kept by Catholic parishes.
- **Important caveat:** Survival varies widely by parish — many Cork Catholic parishes' registers begin only in the 1810s–1830s. Check the specific parish's start date before assuming coverage.
- **Where held:**
  - **Catholic registers:** The National Library of Ireland holds free online digital/microfilm images of Catholic parish registers up to 1880.
  - **Church of Ireland registers:** Held at the Representative Church Body Library or in local custody.

### Census Records
- **Major loss:** Pre-1901 Irish censuses were largely destroyed in the **1922 Four Courts fire**. No 1841 or earlier returns are generally available.
- **Substitutes for census data:**
  - **Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837):** A tax/land-occupancy record — the best substitute for the exact target period.
  - **Griffith's Valuation (early 1850s):** Compiled slightly after the target period but still useful for locating families on the land.

### Land Records
- Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837) double as both a tax record and a land-occupancy survey — the primary land record for this period.

### Immigration/Emigration Records
- **Relevant port:** Cork's ports, specifically **Cobh (then called Queenstown)**.
- **Record types:** Famine-era passenger manifests from Cork ports.
- **Important tip:** These manifests list complete family groups, including infants — examine the whole manifest, not just the head of household.

### Records with Gaps in This Survey
The following were **not addressed** by retrieved sources and should be investigated directly:
- Probate and court records
- Military records
- Cemetery records (a general [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) link was returned, but no Cork-specific index)
- Cork-specific newspaper archives (general [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) was returned)

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Library of Ireland | Catholic parish registers to 1880 (digital/microfilm) | Free online |
| Representative Church Body Library | Church of Ireland parish registers | In-person; some in local custody |
| FamilySearch Wiki | General Ireland genealogy guidance | Free — [Ireland Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy) |

---

## Known Record Losses
Per the [FamilySearch Ireland Genealogy Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy), most pre-1901 Irish census returns — along with many wills and government records — were destroyed in the **1922 Four Courts fire**. The Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation are the standard named substitutes.

---

## Key Research Tips
1. **No civil records exist for this period** — focus on church registers.
2. **Check your ancestor's specific parish**: Catholic register survival varies, and some Cork parishes only begin in the 1820s–1830s.
3. **Use the Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)** as the closest census substitute for the exact target period.
4. **If emigration was through Cork ports**, search Famine-era passenger manifests for the entire family group, not just the head of household.
5. Consult the **National Library of Ireland** and the **FamilySearch Research Wiki** directly to identify which specific Cork parish holdings survive and are digitized.

---

Next, if you'd like, I can build a step-by-step research plan using this guide, or try to pin down the specific parish your ancestor's family belonged to.

The locality guide for **Lincolnshire, England, 1750–1800** has been produced and saved to the project as **loc_001**.

Here is a summary of what the guide covers:

---

## Lincolnshire, England — Christenings & Marriages, 1750–1800

### Key Context
- **No civil registration** existed in England before 1837. For this period, **Church of England parish registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary source.
- **Bishop's Transcripts** (diocesan backup copies) were made annually and serve as a critical fallback when original registers are damaged or missing.
- Physical holdings are at **Lincolnshire Archives**; many volumes have also been digitized by FamilySearch, Findmypast, and Ancestry.

### Critical Warning: Most FamilySearch Lincolnshire Records Are Browse-Only
FamilySearch has **over a thousand digitized volumes** of Lincolnshire parish registers for this period, but the **great majority are unindexed (browse-only)** — meaning you cannot search by name and must page through images manually. Indexed collections do exist but are limited, so plan for image browsing alongside name searches.

### Calendar Note
England adopted the **Gregorian calendar in 1752**, so dates near the start of a year just before that transition can be ambiguous (Old Style vs. New Style). Keep this in mind for records from the early part of this period.

### Repositories
- **Lincolnshire Archives** — primary physical repository
- **FamilySearch** — digitized volumes (many browse-only)
- **Findmypast** — strong Lincolnshire parish register coverage
- **Ancestry** — additional indexed and image collections

### Recommended Next Step
A research plan can now be built from this guide to identify and search the specific Lincolnshire parish and county-wide collections on FamilySearch for the individuals of interest.

quirks: FamilySearch's own indexed christening/marriage/burial collections for England (England Births and Christenings 1538-1975; England Marriages 1538-1973; England Deaths and Burials 1538-1991; Great Britain Births and Baptisms/Marriages/Deaths and Burials) are Legacy Collections per the FamilySearch Wiki England Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records) - each is only a partial index assembled around April 2010, with no further records added or corrections made, so a negative search result in them is not proof the event is unindexed everywhere.

Civil registration in England and Wales did not begin until 1 July 1837, so for 1750-1800 christenings and marriages the Church of England parish register (baptism/marriage/burial) and its Bishop's Transcript are the only vital-event records; there is no civil registration source for this period (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration).

From 1754 (Hardwicke's Marriage Act) parish marriage registers used a printed form and began recording banns separately, residence, marital condition, witnesses and the officiating minister's name - pre-1754 entries are sparser (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).

England changed from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar in September 1752 (11 days dropped) and moved New Year's Day from 25 March to 1 January; pre-1752 dates between 1 Jan and 24 Mar may be double-dated (e.g. 16 February 1696/7) - watch for this across the 1750-1800 window (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).

Many Lincolnshire parishes are small; a village's register may be filed under the mother parish it was a chapelry of rather than its own name - check Lincolnshire Parishes (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincolnshire_Parishes) and the FamilySearch 1851 Jurisdictions map before assuming a register does not exist.

Bishop's Transcripts (annual copies of parish registers sent to the diocese from 1598) can fill gaps where the original Lincolnshire parish register is missing or damaged for 1750-1800, but they are not always exact copies (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).

volume_search returned 1066 digitized Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800; per its summary, of 650 Baptism volumes only 4 are full-text searchable and the rest (645) are browse-only, and of 323 Marriage volumes only 1 is full-text searchable with 320 browse-only - so most Lincolnshire parish register images for this window must be browsed page by page, not name-searched.

Search neighbouring counties as well: Lincolnshire borders Yorkshire, Nottinghamshire, Leicestershire, Rutland, Northamptonshire, Cambridgeshire and Norfolk (per the Lincolnshire, England Genealogy wiki page's boundary description) - a family near the county edge may appear in a neighbouring county's parish registers.

FamilySearch Wiki's Lincolnshire, England research_tips page could not be retrieved for this survey (no page found at county level); only the England-level Research Tips and Strategies page was available.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Lincolnshire is an ancient maritime county; FamilySearch's standard place record dates it "+1801/" (top-level county), but the county itself long predates that and was in existence throughout 1750-1800. It is traditionally divided into the Parts of Holland, Kesteven, and Lindsey, each with its own wapentakes (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincolnshire,_England_Genealogy).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Lincoln.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for "Lincolnshire, England, United Kingdom" for 1750-1800 — this survey could not confirm period population figures from that tool.
- **Economy:** Agricultural county (per the 1870 Imperial Gazetteer extract on the Lincolnshire wiki page); records reflect a rural parish structure of 620 parishes plus extra-parochial places.
- **Religious denominations:** The 1851 religious census cited on the wiki page shows the county overwhelmingly Church of England (657 places of worship) alongside a substantial Methodist presence (462 Wesleyan, 221 Primitive) and smaller Baptist, Quaker, Catholic and other nonconformist congregations — these later (1851) figures are the only breakdown the wiki gives, so earlier (1750-1800) proportions are not separately confirmed (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincolnshire,_England_Genealogy).
- **Key historical events:** No Lincolnshire-specific 1750-1800 historical event affecting records was returned by the tools used in this survey.

## Boundary changes
- This survey found no evidence of a county-level boundary change to Lincolnshire itself during 1750-1800; the county's three historic Parts (Holland, Kesteven, Lindsey) and its ~620 parishes are the relevant sub-jurisdictions for locating records, per the Lincolnshire, England Genealogy wiki page.
- Civil registration districts (used for GRO indexing) were not created until 1837 and do not apply to the 1750-1800 window; for this period records are organized by ecclesiastical parish, not registration district.

args.guideSection:
## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration (state level, England and Wales) began 1 July 1837 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration) — this is after the 1750-1800 target window, so there is no civil registration source for this period.
- **What exists:** None for 1750-1800; see Church records below for the period's actual birth/marriage/death substitute.
- **Where held:** Not applicable to this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church of England parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) and Bishop's Transcripts — see Church records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England (established, the overwhelming majority of parishes); growing Methodist and other nonconformist (Baptist, Independent, Quaker) presence from the 1740s-1780s onward; Roman Catholic recusant congregations persisted under civil disabilities until the Catholic Relief Act of 1829 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages (and, from 1754, separate banns registers), burials. Parish chest records (vestry minutes, poor law/bastardy, settlement and removal, apprenticeship records) also survive for many parishes and name people absent from the main registers.
- **Where held:** Originals are usually held at county record offices (Lincolnshire Archives, http://www.calmview.eu/lincolnshirearchives/calmview/default.aspx) for Anglican registers; nonconformist registers mostly went to The National Archives, with some also at county record offices (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records). FamilySearch holds digitized microfilm images of many Lincolnshire parish registers (see Repository guide).
- **Gaps:** `volume_search` for Lincolnshire 1750-1800 shows the large majority of digitized Baptism (645 of 650) and Marriage (320 of 323) volumes are browse-only, with no name index — see Repository guide for the full count. This survey did not confirm any specific parish register as destroyed or lost.
- **Language:** English (Latin is occasionally found in pre-1700 entries, not generally expected for 1750-1800; see England Naming Customs for Latin name forms, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Naming_Customs).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first UK census was 1801, after this period; no national census exists for 1750-1800.
- **State/provincial census:** None identified for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** None confirmed for Lincolnshire 1750-1800 by the tools used.
- **Access:** Not applicable for this window.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories — `catalog_search` returned items such as "The 1641 royal inquest in Lincolnshire" and Lincolnshire poll tax/probate material, but no 1750-1800-specific probate finding aid was surfaced in this survey's catalog results.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for a specific individual here; both will (testate) and administration (intestate) series existed in this period and should be checked.
- **Date range:** Prerogative Court of Canterbury wills, 1384-1858, are indexed at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/5111/) and cover this period for estates with property in more than one diocese.
- **Where held:** Lincolnshire Archives (diocesan/consistory probate court records) and The National Archives/Ancestry for PCC wills.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds, as is standard in England; this survey did not retrieve a Lincolnshire-specific enclosure/land-survey finding.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by a `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` page in this survey (not separately fetched); `volume_search` shows 4 Land-group volumes among the 1066 Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800, all browse-only.
- **Types:** Deeds, enclosure awards, manorial land records.
- **Where held:** Lincolnshire Archives typically holds deeds and enclosure records for the county (not independently confirmed by a tool in this survey beyond the Archives' general listing).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Seven Years' War (1756-1763) and the American War of Independence (1775-1783) fall within this window.
- **Record types:** `volume_search` found 3 Military-group Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800 (1 browse-only, 2 full-text searchable). Collections_search at the UK level also returned UK, Chelsea Pensioners' Service Records 1760-1913 (person_count 933,550) and UK, British Royal Navy Ships' Musters, 1739-1861 (person_count 279,822), both overlapping this period.
- **Where held:** The National Archives (service/pension records); FamilySearch/Ancestry for the indexed collections above.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not itemized by name in this survey's tool results for 1750-1800 (pre-dates most purpose-built municipal cemeteries, which are mainly a 19th-century development); burial records for this period are in the parish burial register (see Church records).
- **Online coverage:** `volume_search` found 183 Cemetery-group Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800, 181 of them browse-only images.
- **Physical records:** Sexton/parish burial registers at Lincolnshire Archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not itemized by name for this period in this survey's results; `volume_search` lists 3 Newspaper-group Lincolnshire volumes, none flagged full-text or indexed.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed beyond the volume_search entries; the British Newspaper Archive (http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/) was returned among general England links but not Lincolnshire-specific titles for 1750-1800.
- **Content value:** Marriage/death notices for the period would most likely appear only for the gentry/middling sort, given 18th-century newspaper circulation.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston, Lincolnshire, is a historic Lincolnshire port; this survey did not confirm port-specific passenger-list coverage for 1750-1800.
- **Record types:** External-links results returned general collections such as "A List of Emigrants from England to America, 1682-1692, 1718-1759" and "Emigrants in Bondage, 1614-1775" (Ancestry), which overlap the target window but are England-wide, not Lincolnshire-specific.
- **Where held:** The National Archives; Ancestry (subscription) for the indexed collections above.
- **Content note:** When passenger or emigration lists for this period are found, check the full manifest/list for all family members, including young children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Poor rate/parish tax records (parish chest), land tax.
- **Date range:** Not independently dated by a tool for Lincolnshire in this survey beyond the general parish-chest description in England Church Records.
- **Where held:** Lincolnshire Archives.
- **Substitute value:** With no census before 1801 and no civil registration before 1837, parish chest poor-law, settlement, and tax records are the principal substitute for tracking families in 1750-1800; Findmypast's "Lincolnshire Settlement Certificates, 1675-1860" and "Lincolnshire Settlement Examinations, 1721-1861" (returned by external_links_search) directly cover this window.

## Research tips
- Always search both the Church of England parish register and its Bishop's Transcript for the same event — either may preserve an entry missing from the other (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).
- Before 1837, non-Anglicans (other than Jews and Quakers) were generally required to marry in the Church of England, so a nonconformist family's marriage may still appear in the parish register even if their baptisms/burials are in a chapel's own register (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).
- Spelling was phonetic and unstandardized in this period — consult "English Phonetic surname Aliases 1750 to 1800" for likely variant spellings of a target surname (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Naming_Customs).
- England switched from the Julian to Gregorian calendar in September 1752 and moved New Year's Day from 25 March to 1 January — watch for double-dating (e.g., 16 February 1696/7 style) on pre-1752 entries at the edge of this period (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).
- Because most of the 1066 digitized Lincolnshire parish-register volumes for 1750-1800 are browse-only (no name index), plan to browse page-by-page by date rather than relying on a name search.
- If a family is not found in the expected parish, check neighboring Lincolnshire parishes and the registers of adjoining counties (Yorkshire, Nottinghamshire, Leicestershire, Rutland, Northamptonshire, Cambridgeshire, Norfolk).

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |

| FamilySearch | 1066 digitized volumes of Lincolnshire parish/vital/cemetery records covering 1750-1800 (per volume_search); mostly browse-only images | Primary digitized source for parish baptisms, marriages and burials in this period | Free |
| Findmypast | Lincolnshire Parish Registers, 1538-1911; Lincolnshire Marriages and Banns, 1754-1837; Lincolnshire Baptisms; Lincolnshire Burials; Lincolnshire Settlement Certificates, 1675-1860; Lincolnshire Settlement Examinations, 1721-1861; Lincolnshire Poor Law Removals, 1665-1865 (https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/lincolnshire-parish-registers-browse-1538-1911) | Indexed access to Lincolnshire parish registers and poor-law/settlement substitutes for 1750-1800 | Subscription ($) |
| Ancestry | Lincolnshire, England Extracted Church of England Parish Records, 1500s-1800s (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/5900) | Extracted Lincolnshire parish records overlapping this period | Subscription ($) |

This survey covered Lincolnshire, England between 1750 and 1800, looking specifically for baptism and marriage records in FamilySearch's indexed parish-register collections. In that era there was no government registration of births, marriages or deaths in England, so the Church of England's parish baptism, marriage and burial registers (and their diocesan backup copies, called Bishop's Transcripts) are the main surviving records, held physically at Lincolnshire Archives, with many pages also photographed and put online by FamilySearch and by subscription sites like Findmypast and Ancestry. The most important warning is that although FamilySearch has over a thousand digitized volumes of Lincolnshire parish registers for this period, the great majority of them are "browse-only" scanned pages with no name search at all, so finding a specific christening or marriage usually means paging through images rather than typing in a name; it is also worth checking neighbouring counties and the fact that England changed its calendar system in 1752, which can make dates near the start of a year confusing.

Next, a research plan can be built from this guide to search the specific Lincolnshire parish and county-wide collections named here for the people of interest.

quirks: FamilySearch's own indexed christening/marriage/burial collections for England (England Births and Christenings 1538-1975; England Marriages 1538-1973; England Deaths and Burials 1538-1991; Great Britain Births and Baptisms/Marriages/Deaths and Burials) are Legacy Collections per the FamilySearch Wiki England Church Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records) - each is only a partial index assembled around April 2010, with no further records added or corrections made, so a negative search result in them is not proof the event is unindexed everywhere.

Civil registration in England and Wales did not begin until 1 July 1837, so for 1750-1800 christenings and marriages the Church of England parish register (baptism/marriage/burial) and its Bishop's Transcript are the only vital-event records; there is no civil registration source for this period (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration).

From 1754 (Hardwicke's Marriage Act) parish marriage registers used a printed form and began recording banns separately, residence, marital condition, witnesses and the officiating minister's name - pre-1754 entries are sparser (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).

England changed from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar in September 1752 (11 days dropped) and moved New Year's Day from 25 March to 1 January; pre-1752 dates between 1 Jan and 24 Mar may be double-dated (e.g. 16 February 1696/7) - watch for this across the 1750-1800 window (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).

Many Lincolnshire parishes are small; a village's register may be filed under the mother parish it was a chapelry of rather than its own name - check Lincolnshire Parishes (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincolnshire_Parishes) and the FamilySearch 1851 Jurisdictions map before assuming a register does not exist.

Bishop's Transcripts (annual copies of parish registers sent to the diocese from 1598) can fill gaps where the original Lincolnshire parish register is missing or damaged for 1750-1800, but they are not always exact copies (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).

volume_search returned 1066 digitized Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800; per its summary, of 650 Baptism volumes only 4 are full-text searchable and the rest (645) are browse-only, and of 323 Marriage volumes only 1 is full-text searchable with 320 browse-only - so most Lincolnshire parish register images for this window must be browsed page by page, not name-searched.

Search neighbouring counties as well: Lincolnshire borders Yorkshire, Nottinghamshire, Leicestershire, Rutland, Northamptonshire, Cambridgeshire and Norfolk (per the Lincolnshire, England Genealogy wiki page's boundary description) - a family near the county edge may appear in a neighbouring county's parish registers.

FamilySearch Wiki's Lincolnshire, England research_tips page could not be retrieved for this survey (no page found at county level); only the England-level Research Tips and Strategies page was available.

# Locality Guide: Lincolnshire, England (1750-1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Lincolnshire is an ancient maritime county; FamilySearch's standard place record dates it "+1801/" (top-level county), but the county itself long predates that and was in existence throughout 1750-1800. It is traditionally divided into the Parts of Holland, Kesteven, and Lindsey, each with its own wapentakes (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincolnshire,_England_Genealogy).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Lincoln.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for "Lincolnshire, England, United Kingdom" for 1750-1800 — this survey could not confirm period population figures from that tool.
- **Economy:** Agricultural county (per the 1870 Imperial Gazetteer extract on the Lincolnshire wiki page); records reflect a rural parish structure of 620 parishes plus extra-parochial places.
- **Religious denominations:** The 1851 religious census cited on the wiki page shows the county overwhelmingly Church of England (657 places of worship) alongside a substantial Methodist presence (462 Wesleyan, 221 Primitive) and smaller Baptist, Quaker, Catholic and other nonconformist congregations — these later (1851) figures are the only breakdown the wiki gives, so earlier (1750-1800) proportions are not separately confirmed (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Lincolnshire,_England_Genealogy).
- **Key historical events:** No Lincolnshire-specific 1750-1800 historical event affecting records was returned by the tools used in this survey.

## Boundary changes
- This survey found no evidence of a county-level boundary change to Lincolnshire itself during 1750-1800; the county's three historic Parts (Holland, Kesteven, Lindsey) and its ~620 parishes are the relevant sub-jurisdictions for locating records, per the Lincolnshire, England Genealogy wiki page.
- Civil registration districts (used for GRO indexing) were not created until 1837 and do not apply to the 1750-1800 window; for this period records are organized by ecclesiastical parish, not registration district.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration (state level, England and Wales) began 1 July 1837 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Civil_Registration) — this is after the 1750-1800 target window, so there is no civil registration source for this period.
- **What exists:** None for 1750-1800; see Church records below for the period's actual birth/marriage/death substitute.
- **Where held:** Not applicable to this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church of England parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) and Bishop's Transcripts — see Church records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England (established, the overwhelming majority of parishes); growing Methodist and other nonconformist (Baptist, Independent, Quaker) presence from the 1740s-1780s onward; Roman Catholic recusant congregations persisted under civil disabilities until the Catholic Relief Act of 1829 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records).
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages (and, from 1754, separate banns registers), burials. Parish chest records (vestry minutes, poor law/bastardy, settlement and removal, apprenticeship records) also survive for many parishes and name people absent from the main registers.
- **Where held:** Originals are usually held at county record offices (Lincolnshire Archives, http://www.calmview.eu/lincolnshirearchives/calmview/default.aspx) for Anglican registers; nonconformist registers mostly went to The National Archives, with some also at county record offices (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Church_Records). FamilySearch holds digitized microfilm images of many Lincolnshire parish registers (see Repository guide).
- **Gaps:** `volume_search` for Lincolnshire 1750-1800 shows the large majority of digitized Baptism (645 of 650) and Marriage (320 of 323) volumes are browse-only, with no name index — see Repository guide for the full count. This survey did not confirm any specific parish register as destroyed or lost.
- **Language:** English (Latin is occasionally found in pre-1700 entries, not generally expected for 1750-1800; see England Naming Customs for Latin name forms, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/England_Naming_Customs).

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first UK census was 1801, after this period; no national census exists for 1750-1800.
- **State/provincial census:** None identified for this period.
- **Other enumerations:** None confirmed for Lincolnshire 1750-1800 by the tools used.
- **Access:** Not applicable for this window.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories — `catalog_search` returned items such as "The 1641 royal inquest in Lincolnshire" and Lincolnshire poll tax/probate material, but no 1750-1800-specific probate finding aid was surfaced in this survey's catalog results.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not established for a specific individual here; both will (testate) and administration (intestate) series existed in this period and should be checked.
- **Date range:** Prerogative Court of Canterbury wills, 1384-1858, are indexed at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/5111/) and cover this period for estates with property in more than one diocese.
- **Where held:** Lincolnshire Archives (diocesan/consistory probate court records) and The National Archives/Ancestry for PCC wills.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds, as is standard in England; this survey did not retrieve a Lincolnshire-specific enclosure/land-survey finding.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed by a `{Jurisdiction}_Land_and_Property` page in this survey (not separately fetched); `volume_search` shows 4 Land-group volumes among the 1066 Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800, all browse-only.
- **Types:** Deeds, enclosure awards, manorial land records.
- **Where held:** Lincolnshire Archives typically holds deeds and enclosure records for the county (not independently confirmed by a tool in this survey beyond the Archives' general listing).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Seven Years' War (1756-1763) and the American War of Independence (1775-1783) fall within this window.
- **Record types:** `volume_search` found 3 Military-group Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800 (1 browse-only, 2 full-text searchable). Collections_search at the UK level also returned UK, Chelsea Pensioners' Service Records 1760-1913 (person_count 933,550) and UK, British Royal Navy Ships' Musters, 1739-1861 (person_count 279,822), both overlapping this period.
- **Where held:** The National Archives (service/pension records); FamilySearch/Ancestry for the indexed collections above.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not itemized by name in this survey's tool results for 1750-1800 (pre-dates most purpose-built municipal cemeteries, which are mainly a 19th-century development); burial records for this period are in the parish burial register (see Church records).
- **Online coverage:** `volume_search` found 183 Cemetery-group Lincolnshire volumes for 1750-1800, 181 of them browse-only images.
- **Physical records:** Sexton/parish burial registers at Lincolnshire Archives.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Not itemized by name for this period in this survey's results; `volume_search` lists 3 Newspaper-group Lincolnshire volumes, none flagged full-text or indexed.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed beyond the volume_search entries; the British Newspaper Archive (http://www.britishnewspaperarchive.co.uk/) was returned among general England links but not Lincolnshire-specific titles for 1750-1800.
- **Content value:** Marriage/death notices for the period would most likely appear only for the gentry/middling sort, given 18th-century newspaper circulation.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston, Lincolnshire, is a historic Lincolnshire port; this survey did not confirm port-specific passenger-list coverage for 1750-1800.
- **Record types:** External-links results returned general collections such as "A List of Emigrants from England to America, 1682-1692, 1718-1759" and "Emigrants in Bondage, 1614-1775" (Ancestry), which overlap the target window but are England-wide, not Lincolnshire-specific.
- **Where held:** The National Archives; Ancestry (subscription) for the indexed collections above.
- **Content note:** When passenger or emigration lists for this period are found, check the full manifest/list for all family members, including young children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Poor rate/parish tax records (parish chest), land tax.
- **Date range:** Not independently dated by a tool for Lincolnshire in this survey beyond the general parish-chest description in England Church Records.
- **Where held:** Lincolnshire Archives.
- **Substitute value:** With no census before 1801 and no civil registration before 1837, parish chest poor-law, settlement, and tax records are the principal substitute for tracking families in 1750-1800; Findmypast's "Lincolnshire Settlement Certificates, 1675-1860" and "Lincolnshire Settlement Examinations, 1721-1861" (returned by external_links_search) directly cover this window.

### Other record types

---

## Württemberg, Germany — Lutheran Church Records, 1780–1830

### Record-Keeping Context
- **Civil registration did not begin in Württemberg until 1876.** For 1780–1830, the Lutheran church registers are the *only* official source for baptisms, marriages, and burials.
- Lutheran parishes recorded **baptisms** (not births), **marriages**, and **burials** in separate books called *Kirchenbücher*.

### Where the Records Are Held
- **Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart** (Lutheran Church Archive, Stuttgart) holds the original registers.
- **Archion** (subscription-based) provides online browsable images of Württemberg Lutheran church books.
- **FamilySearch** and **Ancestry** hold indexes and some images — though many record sets are image-only (no name index), requiring page-by-page browsing.

### Critical Note on Two Given Names
For this family's children baptised with two given names: German parents of this era commonly used the **second given name** as the child's actual call name throughout life. Confirmation records, marriage entries, and burial records may list only that second name. Always check later records to determine which name the person actually went by — do not assume it was the first name written at baptism.

### Next Steps
The guide recommends building a research plan targeting the family's specific Württemberg parish using the Württemberg Lutheran baptism and marriage collections on FamilySearch and Archion.

args.guideSection:
## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Grafschaft (County) Württemberg existed from 1135, becoming the Duchy of Württemberg in 1495, then the Kingdom of Württemberg from 1806; the modern State of Württemberg, Germany dates 1871-1945 within the German Empire (place_search_all).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Stuttgart.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** For 1780-1830, the Duchy of Württemberg (to 1806) then the Kingdom of Württemberg, within the Holy Roman Empire and then (from 1806) the Confederation of the Rhine/German Confederation.
- **Population during period:** No Württemberg-specific population figure was returned; place_population returned only Germany-wide estimates (c. 18,000,000 in 1800 rising to c. 28,000,000 by 1830) — a Württemberg-level figure was not confirmed by this survey.
- **Economy / Ethnic composition / Religious denominations:** FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched in this survey state that the main religious division in Germany was between Catholics and Protestants (chiefly Lutheran/Evangelisch and Reformed), and that Württemberg family registers (Familienbücher) are especially common after 1808 — a distinctly Württemberg/Baden practice (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records). No tool result in this survey gave Württemberg-specific economy or ethnic-composition detail.
- **Key historical events:** Napoleonic-era territorial reorganization (Württemberg became a Kingdom in 1806); areas of Germany under French control in the early 1800s sometimes kept records in French (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).

## Boundary changes
- Württemberg's jurisdictional status changed from County (to 1495) to Duchy (1495-1806) to Kingdom (1806-1918) to State within the German Empire (1871-1945, per place_search_all's standard-place record), continuing today as part of Baden-Württemberg (since 1945).
- All German genealogical records are catalogued by FamilySearch under the place names in use at the 1871 German Empire unification (Meyers Orts- und Verkehrslexikon, "Meyer's Gazetteer") — this is the system still used in the FamilySearch Catalog and FamilySearch Historical Records today (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Württemberg,_Germany_Genealogy). For an 1780-1830 family, search under the parish's 1871-era name/jurisdiction, not a modern municipality name.
- This is a temporal/administrative renaming, not a geographic split — records for a given town stay with that town's parish across these changes; the quirk is which place-name index term to use, not which of two successor jurisdictions holds the record.

args.guideSection:
### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Lutheran (Evangelisch) churches generally began requiring registers around 1540; Catholic parish records were mandated in 1563; by 1650 most Reformed parishes kept records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records). Württemberg's Evangelical Lutheran church is organized under the Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart; a Catholic diocese for the area is Rottenburg-Stuttgart (per the "Germany, Württemberg, Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart, Catholic Church Records, 1520-1975" collection, id 3499252).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (Taufen), marriages (Heiraten) including banns (Aufgebote), burials (Begräbnisse), confirmations (Konfirmationen), and — distinctively for Württemberg and Baden after 1808 — family registers (Familienbücher) compiling a household's births, marriages and deaths (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Catalog (digitized microfilm, mixed indexed/browse-only, see Available record types/volumes below); Archion (subscription online images of Lutheran originals, held by the Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart); Ancestry's "Württemberg, Germany, Lutheran Baptisms, Marriages, and Burials, 1500-1985" (subscription). Duplicate yearly copies (Kirchenbuchduplikate), where made, are generally in central church or state archives rather than the local parish.
- **Gaps:** This survey found no Württemberg-specific record-loss statement; the general German-wide note is that many church records were destroyed in the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) and some Lutheran records in areas later ceded to Poland were lost in WWII — neither applies directly to Württemberg 1780-1830 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Language:** Protestant (Lutheran) registers were usually written in German; Catholic registers in Latin or German. Areas under French control in the early 1800s sometimes have records in French.

# Locality Guide: Württemberg, Germany (1780-1830)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The Grafschaft (County) Württemberg existed from 1135, becoming the Duchy of Württemberg in 1495, then the Kingdom of Württemberg from 1806; the modern State of Württemberg, Germany dates 1871-1945 within the German Empire (place_search_all).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Stuttgart.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** For 1780-1830, the Duchy of Württemberg (to 1806) then the Kingdom of Württemberg, within the Holy Roman Empire and then (from 1806) the Confederation of the Rhine/German Confederation.
- **Population during period:** No Württemberg-specific population figure was returned; place_population returned only Germany-wide estimates (c. 18,000,000 in 1800 rising to c. 28,000,000 by 1830) — a Württemberg-level figure was not confirmed by this survey.
- **Economy / Ethnic composition / Religious denominations:** FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched in this survey state that the main religious division in Germany was between Catholics and Protestants (chiefly Lutheran/Evangelisch and Reformed), and that Württemberg family registers (Familienbücher) are especially common after 1808 — a distinctly Württemberg/Baden practice (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records). No tool result in this survey gave Württemberg-specific economy or ethnic-composition detail.
- **Key historical events:** Napoleonic-era territorial reorganization (Württemberg became a Kingdom in 1806); areas of Germany under French control in the early 1800s sometimes kept records in French (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).

## Boundary changes
- Württemberg's jurisdictional status changed from County (to 1495) to Duchy (1495-1806) to Kingdom (1806-1918) to State within the German Empire (1871-1945, per place_search_all's standard-place record), continuing today as part of Baden-Württemberg (since 1945).
- All German genealogical records are catalogued by FamilySearch under the place names in use at the 1871 German Empire unification (Meyers Orts- und Verkehrslexikon, "Meyer's Gazetteer") — this is the system still used in the FamilySearch Catalog and FamilySearch Historical Records today (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Württemberg,_Germany_Genealogy). For an 1780-1830 family, search under the parish's 1871-era name/jurisdiction, not a modern municipality name.
- This is a temporal/administrative renaming, not a geographic split — records for a given town stay with that town's parish across these changes; the quirk is which place-name index term to use, not which of two successor jurisdictions holds the record.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Statewide civil registration began 1 January 1876 across the German Empire including Württemberg (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Civil_Registration) — this postdates the 1780-1830 target window entirely.
- **What exists for 1780-1830:** None at the civil (Standesamt) level; the period is covered only by church records.
- **Where held:** Not applicable for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Lutheran (and Catholic) parish registers are the primary vital-record source for 1780-1830 — see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Lutheran (Evangelisch) churches generally began requiring registers around 1540; Catholic parish records were mandated in 1563; by 1650 most Reformed parishes kept records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records). Württemberg's Evangelical Lutheran church is organized under the Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart; a Catholic diocese for the area is Rottenburg-Stuttgart (per the "Germany, Württemberg, Diocese of Rottenburg-Stuttgart, Catholic Church Records, 1520-1975" collection, id 3499252).
- **Record types:** Baptisms (Taufen), marriages (Heiraten) including banns (Aufgebote), burials (Begräbnisse), confirmations (Konfirmationen), and — distinctively for Württemberg and Baden after 1808 — family registers (Familienbücher) compiling a household's births, marriages and deaths (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Catalog (digitized microfilm, mixed indexed/browse-only, see Available record types/volumes below); Archion (subscription online images of Lutheran originals, held by the Landeskirchliches Archiv Stuttgart); Ancestry's "Württemberg, Germany, Lutheran Baptisms, Marriages, and Burials, 1500-1985" (subscription). Duplicate yearly copies (Kirchenbuchduplikate), where made, are generally in central church or state archives rather than the local parish.
- **Gaps:** This survey found no Württemberg-specific record-loss statement; the general German-wide note is that many church records were destroyed in the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) and some Lutheran records in areas later ceded to Poland were lost in WWII — neither applies directly to Württemberg 1780-1830 (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Church_Records).
- **Language:** Protestant (Lutheran) registers were usually written in German; Catholic registers in Latin or German. Areas under French control in the early 1800s sometimes have records in French.

### Census records
- **National/state census:** No national German census existed in this period; FamilySearch Wiki states German censuses were taken only locally by some states/provinces/cities, and are generally less useful than church/civil records (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Census). The survey found no Württemberg-specific census collection.
- **Other enumerations:** None confirmed for Württemberg 1780-1830 in this survey; the fetched Census page details Mecklenburg-Schwerin, Prussian Saxony, Schleswig-Holstein and Lübeck censuses, none of which apply to Württemberg.
- **Access:** Not applicable — use parish family registers (Familienbücher) as the Württemberg substitute for household-level enumeration.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** A dedicated Württemberg probate collection was found: "Germany, Württemberg, Schwäbisch Hall, Probate Records, 1803-1929" (collection id 1475994, person count not available from the index).

- **Where held:** Catalogued at FamilySearch; browse/index status for this specific collection was not confirmed by volume_search.

### Land records

- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** This survey did not confirm it — Germany_Land_and_Property was not fetched in this pass.
- **Types / Date range / Where held:** volume_search's record-type summary lists 19 "Land" volumes in its Württemberg 1780-1830 results, all browse-only, with no further detail returned about titles or places; this survey did not confirm specifics.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Württemberg was drawn into the Napoleonic Wars (as a Napoleonic ally after 1806) within this period.
- **Record types:** The external_links_search results list "Germany & Austria, Directories of Military and Marine Officers, 1500-1939" and "Germany and Austria, Military and Marine Unit Histories, 1760-1933" (Ancestry, subscription) as the only period-overlapping military resources returned; volume_search's summary shows only 1 Military-group volume (browse-only) for Württemberg 1780-1830.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** None named for Württemberg by any tool result in this survey.
- **Online coverage:** external_links_search returned general German resources — BillionGraves (country-wide search page) and the German "Grabsteine" (gravestone) site by genealogy.net, with a "Grabsteine: nach Bundesländern" (by federal state) index page.

### Newspaper records

- **Content value:** Not confirmed for this period and place by this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Not directly on a coast; emigrants from Württemberg typically emigrated overland then via ports such as Bremen or le Havre — no specific port confirmed for this family by any tool result.
- **Record types:** external_links_search returned "Württemberg, Germany Emigration Index, 1808-1890" (Ancestry) and "Auswanderung aus Südwestdeutschland, 1751-1920" (emigration from southwest Germany database) — both overlap the later target years (1808-1830).
- **Where held:** Ancestry (subscription) and the auswanderer-bw.de database (free).
- **Content note:** Passenger manifests, when found, list every traveling family member including infants — check the full manifest for all family members, not just the presumed head of household.

### Tax records
- **Types:** volume_search's summary lists 100 Tax-group volumes for Württemberg 1780-1830, all browse-only (not name-indexed, not full-text searchable).
- **Date range:** Not individually itemized by the summary call; the window searched was 1780-1830.

Here is the locality guide for **Kolonica, Slovakia**:

---

## Kolonica — Locality Guide (1700s–1890s)

### Jurisdictional Context
Kolonica is a small village now located in the **Snina district of northeastern Slovakia**. During the entire period you are researching (1700s–1890s), it was part of **Zemplén County in the Kingdom of Hungary**, not Slovakia. This is crucial for research because records were kept in Latin and Hungarian under Hungarian ecclesiastical and civil administration.

### Church Records

**Denomination:** Greek Catholic — this was the dominant rite in the Greek Catholic Greek-rite communities of Zemplén County.

**What survives online (FamilySearch):**
- **Greek Catholic parish register for Kolonica** — covers:
  - Baptisms, marriages, and deaths: **1824–1833**
  - Baptisms, marriages, and deaths: **1890–1924**
- Written in **Latin and Hungarian**
- These registers were microfilmed from a state archive at **Levoča** (the Slovak National Archive branch)

**Gaps and Limitations:**
- **No records found online for the 1700s or early 1800s** (before 1824) — the earliest part of your target period is not yet covered by digitized sources
- There is an **unexplained gap from 1834 to 1889** in what has been filmed or survived — roughly 55 years in the middle of your window
- The gap may reflect lost originals, unfilmed registers, or records held at the Levoča archive but not yet digitized

### Where to Look Next

| Priority | Repository | What to Seek |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | FamilySearch (online) | Search the 1824–1833 and 1890–1924 Kolonica registers now available |
| 2 | **Štátny archív v Levoči** (State Archive, Levoča) | Inquire about any earlier volumes and the 1834–1889 gap — original registers were sourced from here |
| 3 | Greek Catholic diocese archives | May hold bishop's registers or duplicates that fill gaps |

### Research Notes
- Civil registration in Hungary did not begin until **1895**, so for the entire pre-1895 period you are entirely dependent on church registers
- The Greek Catholic parish structure in Zemplén County was organized under the **Diocese of Mukachevo** (Munkács) — diocesan archives in Uzhhorod, Ukraine may also hold relevant records
- Neighboring parishes may have served Kolonica residents during periods when the local register is missing

---

**Next step:** A research plan can be built from this guide to search the 1824–1833 and 1890–1924 Kolonica registers now online, and to contact the Levoča archive about earlier and gap-period volumes.

# Locality Guide: Berkshire County, Massachusetts (1820–1850)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Formed:** 1761, in the far western part of Massachusetts
- **Border geography:** Sits along both the New York and Vermont state lines — families there commonly generated records across all three states
- **Key context:** Massachusetts vital-record-keeping was local (town clerk) throughout most of this period; statewide civil registration didn't begin until **1841**, and Boston was excluded until 1850

## Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**What exists:**
- For **1820–1840**: Only town-clerk-level records. Each individual town kept its own birth, marriage, and death registers.
- For **1841–1850**: Both town-level and state-level records co-exist.
- **Marriage intentions** were commonly recorded in the bride's home town, with possible duplicate recordings in the groom's town and their town of residence — search all relevant towns.

**Where to look:**
- **FamilySearch** — "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890" (collection id 2061550) — free, covers this period
- **Physical originals** remain with individual town clerks (Berkshire County towns)
- **Massachusetts State Archives** holds state-level records from 1841 onward

## Church Records
A **Pittsfield Congregational church register (1791–1850)** was specifically identified (FamilySearch image group 004500892, 274 images). This covers baptisms, marriages, and burials.

⚠️ **Important:** This volume is **0% name-indexed** — it cannot be searched by name. You must browse it page by page on FamilySearch.

FamilySearch's broader **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (collection id 1921657) also covers the state and period.

## Other Key Record Types

| Record Type | Collection | Repository | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Probate (wills, administrations) | Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991 (id 1678901) | FamilySearch | Free |
| Naturalization | Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906 (id 1459213) | FamilySearch | Free |
| Federal Census | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1820, 1830, 1840, 1850) | Ancestry / FamilySearch | Subscription/Free |
| Cemetery records | — | Find A Grave (findagrave.com) | Free |
| Military records | — | Fold3 (fold3.com); NARA (archives.gov) | Subscription/Free |
| Newspapers | — | Newspapers.com | Subscription |
| Land/Deeds | Registry of Deeds, county level | Berkshire County Registry | In-person |

## Records NOT Yet Online
Most town-level vital records for Berkshire County towns **outside Pittsfield** were not found in a digitized/indexed form in this survey. Land/deed records and much of the probate detail may require a courthouse visit or written request to the **Berkshire County Registry of Probate/Deeds**.

## Research Tips for This Area

1. **Cross state lines**: Because the family's town is near New York and Vermont, check adjoining counties in both states — they may have worshipped, married, or done business just across the border.
2. **Town catalog searches**: A direct FamilySearch Catalog search at the county level returned no hits in this survey. Try searching by **individual town name** in the FamilySearch Catalog, since microfilm holdings are often cataloged at the town level.
3. **Browse-only volumes**: The Pittsfield town-clerk and Congregational church volumes found here require page-by-page browsing — budget extra time for this.
4. **1841 cutoff**: For events before 1841, rely exclusively on town clerk and church records; state-level recording simply didn't exist yet.
5. **Marriage intentions**: Check the bride's town, groom's town, *and* residence town for marriage intention records.

---

Once you've identified the specific town, I can build a targeted research plan from this guide. Would you like to do that?

## Boundary changes
No boundary changes for Berkshire County itself were returned by the tools used in this survey; `place_search` shows it continuously existing from 1761 forward. No evidence of a split or re-parenting during 1820–1850 was found.

- **Start date:** According to the FamilySearch Wiki page "Massachusetts Vital Records" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records), Massachusetts was the first state to create a permanent, statewide recording system, beginning in **1841** — but the city of Boston was excluded until **1850**. Before and alongside that, vital records were created and kept by the **town or city clerk** where the event occurred; an early colonial county-level copying practice "died out before 1800."
- **What exists:** For your 1820–1850 window, expect **town-clerk-level** birth, marriage, and death entries for the whole period, plus **state-level** records only from 1841 onward. Marriage intentions were commonly recorded in the bride's home town, with additional recordings possibly in the groom's town and their town of residence — check all three towns.
- **Where held:** Originals remain with the town/city clerk per the Wiki page above. FamilySearch's collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection id 2061550, ~3,456,789 people) covers this period and record level.
- **Gaps:** No specific Berkshire County vital-record losses were identified by this survey.
- **Pre/alongside-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below) and marriage intentions filed in multiple towns.

### Church records

**Locality Research Guide — Jalisco, Mexico, 1880–1920**

**Civil Registration**
Jalisco municipios have kept civil registers of births, marriages, and deaths from 1859 onward; practical compliance became reliable after 1867. Records were maintained at the local municipio level. Notarial records and most land records from this era are not yet name-indexed and must be browsed as images.

Use this guide as the basis for a research plan targeting the specific Jalisco civil-registration and parish collections most relevant to this family.

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Jalisco became the 9th state of Mexico on 23 December 1823 (Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy).
- **Capital:** Guadalajara.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexico (national).
- **Population during period:** state estimates of 983,500 (1882), 1,161,700 (1889), 1,250,000 (1892), 1,107,200 (1896), 1,153,900 (1900) and 1,208,900 (1910) (populstat, via place_population). National population rose from about 10.26 million (1880) to about 14.57 million (1920) (Gapminder, via place_population).
- **Economy:** Agricultural hacienda economy around Guadalajara and the Los Altos region, shaping landholding and notarial records.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly mestizo/Spanish-descended population, with Huichol and Nahua indigenous communities and a smaller Otomí presence (Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy).
- **Religious denominations:** Overwhelmingly Roman Catholic, administered by the Archdiocese of Guadalajara.
- **Key historical events:** The 1910-1920 Mexican Revolution falls within the target period and disrupted civil administration in parts of the state in its later years.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration (Registro Civil) was established nationally on 28 July 1859 by presidential decree, but was widely resisted and not vigorously enforced until the republic was restored in 1867 (Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration). Treat 1859-1867 coverage as partial.
- **What exists:** Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 (FamilySearch collection 1918187; index & images; 28,607,850 people) covers births, marriages, and deaths at the municipio level (collections_search). Ancestry separately hosts Jalisco, Mexico, Civil Registration Births 1857-1948, Marriages 1861-1961, and Deaths 1856-1987 (subscription; Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy page).
- **Where held:** Kept at the municipio (local civil registration office) level throughout Jalisco — unlike Guerrero, Oaxaca (district level) or the Distrito Federal (delegation level) (Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).
- **Gaps:** This survey did not confirm specific missing years for individual Jalisco municipios; `volume_search` shows most 1880-1920 vital-record volumes in the Vital group (7,774 volumes) are either indexed or full-text searchable, with only 7 browse-only and 27 full-text-only noted in that count.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic parish baptism, marriage, and burial registers, which continued in parallel after 1859 (see Church records below).

- **Record types:** Baptisms (bautismos), marriages, burials, and marriage dispensations. `volume_search` lists individual parish baptism libros for 1880-1920, e.g. Sagrario Metropolitano, Guadalajara libros 49 (1888-1889) and 50 (1889-1893), each 100% name-indexed, and San Agustín, Tlajomulco de Zúñiga libros 1-4 (1913-1922), 97-99% indexed with libro 1 also full-text searchable.

- **Language:** Spanish, with Latin in some earlier entries (e.g. Sagrario Metropolitano libros 49-50 are recorded in Spanish and Latin, per volume_search).

## Records NOT online
- Notarial records (350 volumes in the 1880-1920 `volume_search` count) are entirely full-text-only or browse, not name-indexed, so they cannot be found by a standard name search — they must be read.
- Land/property records for this period (only 2 volumes found, both full-text-only) are not name-searchable online.
- Tax records specific to Jalisco were not located online in this survey at all — this is a gap, not evidence they don't exist; check physical archives directly.
- Divorce records are not part of civil registration in Mexico (divorce was handled by municipio courts and only legalized after the 1917 constitution) and the FamilySearch Library holds very few divorce records (Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration) — contact the municipio court directly.

args.guideSection:
## Research tips
- Because the family used two surnames, search FamilySearch and Ancestry indexes using only the paternal (first) surname — most records are indexed on that surname alone, per "Improve your Search Results for Hispanic Ancestors in FamilySearch.org" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org).
- Women are recorded under their maiden surname in civil, church, and legal records even after marriage, per Mexico Naming Customs (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs) — search a wife by her birth surname, not her husband's.
- Search both the civil registration (from 1859) and the parallel Catholic parish registers for the same birth, marriage, or death — the two series can each contain details missing from the other, per Mexico Civil Registration (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).
- When a birth, marriage, or death is not found, search neighboring municipios and parishes, and search siblings' births and parents' marriages to build out the family, per the Mexico Research Tips and Strategies page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Research_Tips_and_Strategies).
- Use wildcard characters and spelling variants when searching indexed names, and prefer the broad "Any" life-event filter over narrowing to Births/Marriages/Deaths individually, per the Hispanic Ancestors search-tips page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org).
- If a record is not yet indexed, browse the collection by selecting Jalisco, then the municipio or parish, then the record type and year, per the same Hispanic Ancestors search-tips page.

This survey looked at the state of Jalisco in western Mexico for the years 1880 to 1920, the period when a family using two surnames would have generated birth and marriage paperwork there. Civil registration offices in Jalisco kept births, marriages and deaths at the local municipio level from 1859 onward (though compliance only became reliable after 1867), and the Catholic Church kept its own parallel baptism and marriage registers through the Archdiocese of Guadalajara; both sets of records are substantially digitized and searchable online through FamilySearch and, by subscription, through Ancestry, though a meaningful share of the parish registers and virtually all of the notarial and land records from this era are not yet searchable by name and must be browsed image by image. The single biggest practical warning is that, because the family carried two surnames in the Spanish style, most indexed records list only the father's surname, so searches should be run on that surname alone, and a married woman will appear under her own maiden surname, never her husband's, in every record type.

Next, the research-plan step should use this guide to lay out which specific Jalisco civil-registration and parish collections to search first for this family.

quirks: Hispanic double-surname families are usually indexed in FamilySearch and Ancestry under only the paternal (first) surname — search with just the paternal surname, per 'Improve your Search Results for Hispanic Ancestors in FamilySearch.org' (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Improve_your_Search_Results_for_Hispanic_Ancestors_in_FamilySearch.org).

Civil registration in Mexico is kept at the municipio level in nearly every state, including Jalisco; Guerrero, Oaxaca (district level) and Distrito Federal (delegation level) are the stated exceptions, per the Mexico Civil Registration page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Both civil and Catholic Church marriage/baptism/burial records continued to be kept in parallel after 1859 — search both series for the same event, per the Mexico Civil Registration page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration).

Women keep their maiden surname after marriage in Catholic, public, legal and especially civil records — never assume a wife's surname changed, per Mexico Naming Customs (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Naming_Customs).

The 'Jalisco_Vital_Records' and 'Jalisco_Church_Records' pages were not found in the FamilySearch Wiki corpus for this survey; use the state-level Mexico_Vital_Records/Mexico_Church_Records pages and the Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy page instead.

# Locality Guide: Jalisco, Mexico (1880-1920)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Jalisco became the 9th state of Mexico on 23 December 1823 (Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy).
- **Capital:** Guadalajara.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mexico (national).
- **Population during period:** state estimates of 983,500 (1882), 1,161,700 (1889), 1,250,000 (1892), 1,107,200 (1896), 1,153,900 (1900) and 1,208,900 (1910) (populstat, via place_population). National population rose from about 10.26 million (1880) to about 14.57 million (1920) (Gapminder, via place_population).
- **Economy:** Agricultural hacienda economy around Guadalajara and the Los Altos region, shaping landholding and notarial records.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly mestizo/Spanish-descended population, with Huichol and Nahua indigenous communities and a smaller Otomí presence (Jalisco, Mexico Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Jalisco,_Mexico_Genealogy).
- **Religious denominations:** Overwhelmingly Roman Catholic, administered by the Archdiocese of Guadalajara.
- **Key historical events:** The 1910-1920 Mexican Revolution falls within the target period and disrupted civil administration in parts of the state in its later years.

## Boundary changes
- Jalisco's borders as a state have been stable since 1823 (place_search dateRange "+1823/"); this survey found no county/municipio-level boundary changes reported for the 1880-1920 window.
- Individual municipios can still have local renamings — e.g. the catalog entry for Atemajac notes the municipio was named "Atemajac de las Tablas" until a 25 April 1903 decree renamed it "Atemajac de Brizuela" (FamilySearch Catalog koha:666457). Confirm the municipio name in use at the record's date before searching.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration (Registro Civil) was established nationally on 28 July 1859 by presidential decree, but was widely resisted and not vigorously enforced until the republic was restored in 1867 (Mexico Civil Registration, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mexico_Civil_Registration). Treat 1859-1867 coverage as partial.
- **What exists:** Mexico, Jalisco, Civil Registration, 1857-2000 (FamilySearch collection 1918187; index & images; 28,607,850 people) covers births, marriages, and deaths at the municipio level (collections_search). This survey covered Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania for the years 1840 to 1880, the county where Patrick Flynn is believed to have died, and it found old records of several kinds: digitized probate, naturalization, church, deed, and marriage volumes held by FamilySearch, plus a federal census collection and an older tax list on Ancestry. # Locality Guide: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (1840-1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1811 (per place_search, dateRange "+1811/") — the Wiki's own jurisdiction narrative (parent counties, county seat, population, economy, ethnic composition, religion, key events) could not be confirmed in this survey: every FamilySearch Wiki page requested for this place or for Pennsylvania returned the same generic placeholder content with no place-specific detail (see quirks). Outside knowledge is not substituted here.
- **County seat / administrative center:** not confirmed by this survey's tool results
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania, United States
- **Population during period:** place_population returned no data for this place/period in this survey
- **Economy / Ethnic composition / Religious denominations / Key historical events:** not confirmed by this survey's tool results — for the history behind the records, consult the historical-context skill

## Boundary changes
- place_search_all returned no historical-jurisdiction data for Schuylkill County; place_search gives a single formation date of 1811 with no parent-county name confirmed by a tool result in this survey. No boundary changes during 1840-1880 were found or ruled out — this could not be confirmed.
