### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Not confirmed — the FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania/Schuylkill vital-records pages returned only generic placeholder content in this survey (no Pennsylvania-specific start year or level), so no date is reported rather than guessed.
- **What exists:** `volume_search` found one browse-only marriage-records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936753) covering 1870-1910, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — outside the 1840-1880 window for most of its range but overlapping its tail end.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized, unindexed images); `collections_search` found no indexed PA-wide vital-records collection for this place.
- **Gaps:** No 1840-1869 marriage or any birth/death volume was found in this survey.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (below) are the main substitute for 1840-1870.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not named by a tool result in this survey; `collections_search` returned a "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" collection (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, 1708-1985, 982,415 persons) but without denomination detail.
- **Record types:** `volume_search` found one browse-only church-records volume (imageGroupNumber 007936751, 187 images, 1842-1895), languages English and German.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized, unindexed) for the volume above; the SYNTH-PA-CHURCH collection above for the broader date range.
- **Gaps:** Which denominations/years are and are not covered could not be confirmed — the FamilySearch Wiki church-records page returned only generic content.
- **Language:** The 1842-1895 volume is partly in German — plan to read original-language entries.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** `external_links_search` surfaced the "1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County" on Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/1276/). No FamilySearch-indexed federal census collection for this county/period was returned by `collections_search`.

- **Other enumerations:** None found; mortality schedules were not confirmed for this place by any tool result.
- **Access:** The Ancestry 1850 census collection above (subscription); no browse-only or indexed FamilySearch census volume for 1840-1880 was returned by `volume_search`.

- **Types:** `volume_search` found one browse-only probate volume (imageGroupNumber 007936749, 412 images, 1851-1930) and one browse-only naturalization volume (007936750, 298 images, 1849-1915); `collections_search` also lists "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196, personCount 0).

- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized, unindexed, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) — must be browsed image by image.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not confirmed by a tool result in this survey.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Not confirmed — the FamilySearch Wiki Land and Property page returned only generic placeholder content.

- **Date range:** 1815-1900, covering the full 1840-1880 target window.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (digitized, partially indexed images).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** The Mexican-American War (1846-1848) and the Civil War (1861-1865) fall within 1840-1880, but no record type, collection, or volume for them was returned by any tool in this survey.

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Location:** Barony of Lower Dunluce (chiefly) and Carey, Poor Law Union of Coleraine, County Antrim, Province of Ulster. Contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunseverick.
- **After 1922:** Part of Northern Ireland, United Kingdom (political change only; no civil-parish boundary change confirmed).
- **Religious composition:** Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic, Presbyterian, Covenanter, and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses all existed in the parish. County Antrim was majority Protestant (Church of Ireland + Presbyterian), with Catholics a substantial minority.

---

## Vital Records (Civil Registration)
| Event | Registration started |
|---|---|
| Protestant marriages | 1845 |
| All births, deaths, all marriages | 1864 |

**Gap:** For 1780–1844 (all events) and 1780–1863 (Catholic/other marriages), there is **no civil registration** — church registers are the primary source.

Post-1864 civil records for Northern Ireland are held by **GRONI** (General Register Office for Northern Ireland) and **PRONI** (see repositories below).

---

## Church Records

### What was found online
Two digitized but **unindexed** volumes for Ballylinny (within Billy parish) were found on FamilySearch — full-text searchable but requiring page-by-page browsing, not name-index searching:

| Volume | Years | Images |
|---|---|---|
| Christenings, Ballylinny | 1837–1868 | 65, 0% name-indexed |
| Marriage Records, Ballylinny | 1837–1864 | 50, 0% name-indexed |

### The gap: Catholic, Presbyterian, Covenanter, Methodist registers
No Catholic, Presbyterian, Covenanter, or Methodist register for Billy/Ballylinny appeared in catalog or collections searches — these likely survive only on paper/microfilm at the repositories listed below.

### Known losses
Two-thirds of Church of Ireland parish registers nationally were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin. Whether Billy's Church of Ireland registers are among the losses or survivors must be confirmed at PRONI or the RCB Library.

### Denominational start dates (Ireland-wide context)
- **Church of Ireland:** Registers begin as early as 1536 — but two-thirds destroyed 1922.
- **Catholic:** Most rural parishes did not begin keeping registers until Catholic Emancipation (**1828**); city parishes from the 1750s.
- **Presbyterian:** Average start date **1830** (variable).
- **Methodist:** Irish society activity from 1746.

---

## Closing the Church-Register Gap: Repositories & Indexes

## Other Record Types

### Census Substitutes (no pre-1901 census survives)

### School Records

### Probate

### Cemetery / Newspaper
- Find A Grave: https://www.findagrave.com/
- Newspapers.com: https://www.newspapers.com/

## Research Tips
1. **Denomination first:** Identify the family's church before searching — each denomination's registers are held and indexed separately, and searches that ignore denomination waste time.
2. **Catholic boundary mismatch:** Catholic parish boundaries did not match civil-parish boundaries — search surrounding parishes if the expected parish yields nothing.
3. **FamilySearch volumes are browse-only:** Use the full-text search tool or plan to browse page by page; name-index searches will return nothing for the two Billy/Ballylinny volumes.
4. **Write to PRONI first:** Their "Guide to Church Records" is the single most direct way to establish which Billy-parish church registers survive and in what form — this is the highest-priority step for closing the unindexed-register gap.
5. **Use Griffith's + Tithe Applotments** for 1820s–1840s when church registers are silent.
6. **1922 fire awareness:** Even where Church of Ireland registers are listed, check whether they are originals, transcripts, or Betham/Crossle/Thrift abstracts — compiled before the fire and therefore valid substitutes.

# Locality Guide: Billy Civil Parish, County Antrim, Ireland (1780–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** An ancient civil parish, partly in the barony of Carey but chiefly in the barony of Lower Dunluce, Poor Law Union of Coleraine, County Antrim, Province of Ulster. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)
- **County seat / administrative center:** The parish contains the post town of Bushmills and part of Dunseverick; the Poor Law Union seat is Coleraine. (same page)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** County Antrim, Province of Ulster; from 1922 within Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** Not returned by this survey — `place_population` returned no data for Billy at this place level, and the generic FamilySearch Wiki pages fetched for County Antrim at `getting_started`/`online_records`/`research_tips` returned only boilerplate content, not Antrim-specific figures. Treat population figures as an open gap.
- **Religious composition:** The parish was formerly the head of an ecclesiastical union also comprising Armoy, Ballyclug, Donegore, and Kilbride, forming the corps of the archdeaconry of Connor; the rectory/vicarage of Billy alone now forms the archdeaconry's corps. In Roman Catholic divisions, Billy falls in the district of Coleraine. Meeting houses existed in the parish for Presbyterians, Covenanters, and Wesleyan Methodists. (Billy Civil Parish wiki page, same URL as above)
- **Key historical events:** County Antrim in this period was predominantly Protestant (Church of Ireland and Presbyterian made up roughly sixty percent of Ulster's population in 1861, with Catholics about forty percent) — this bears directly on which denomination's registers to prioritize. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)

## Boundary changes
- The civil parish of Billy itself is not reported as having been subdivided or re-parented within 1780–1870; `place_search` returns it consistently as "Billy, County Antrim, Ireland" for this era, becoming part of "Northern Ireland, United Kingdom" only after 1922 (administrative/political change, not a boundary change in the parish itself).
- Catholic parish boundaries differed from Church of Ireland civil-parish boundaries throughout this period — the Wiki's Ireland Church Records search strategy explicitly warns researchers to check surrounding localities because "Catholics had different parish boundaries to the Church of Ireland." (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)
- No other boundary change for Billy was identified by this survey; this should be treated as unconfirmed rather than definitively stable, since `place_population` and the generic county-level wiki pages gave no Antrim-specific detail.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Government (state-level) registration of births and deaths in Ireland, including Billy parish, began in **1864**. Registration of **Protestant** marriages began in **1845**, with registration of all marriages compulsory by **1864**. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)
- **What exists:** For 1780–1870, only the final six years (1864–1870) of the target window fall under full civil registration; 1845–1863 covers Protestant marriages only. The bulk of the period (1780–1844 for all events, 1780–1863 for Catholic/other marriages) has **no civil registration** — church registers are the primary source.
- **Where held:** Post-1864 civil records for this parish (Northern Ireland) are held by the **General Register Office for Northern Ireland (GRONI)**; see also PRONI, below.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Church registers (see next section) are the primary source for 1780–1863/1844.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of Ireland, Roman Catholic, Presbyterian, Covenanter, and Wesleyan Methodist meeting houses all existed within Billy parish. (Billy Civil Parish wiki page)
- **Record types:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers are the most common; Catholic and Presbyterian registers frequently lack burial registers. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)
- **Denominational start dates (Ireland-wide, cite per denomination):**
  - Church of Ireland records began in 1536, but **two-thirds were destroyed in the 1922 Public Record Office fire in Dublin.**
  - Catholic registers generally began from the mid-1700s, but most rural parishes did not start keeping registers until Catholic Emancipation in **1828**; city registers can date from the 1750s.
  - Presbyterian registers date variably from the 1600s, but the **average starting date is 1830**.
  - Methodist society activity in Ireland began in Dublin in 1746.
  (All from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records)
- **Digitized holdings found for Billy parish specifically** (via `volume_search`):
  - Christenings, Ballylinny (within Billy parish), **1837–1868** — image group 007907410_008_M9VF-SK5, 65 images, full-text searchable but **0% name-indexed**.
  - Marriage Records, Ballylinny, **1837–1864** — image group 007765074_009_M9VX-Q7W, 50 images, full-text searchable, **0% name-indexed**.
  These two volumes are **browse/full-text only, not name-searchable** — a researcher must search the full text or browse image by image, not rely on a name index.
- **Gaps:** No Catholic, Presbyterian, Covenanter, or Methodist register for Billy/Ballylinny turned up in `collections_search` (0 results) or `catalog_search` (0 hits) in this survey — this is a cataloguing/digitization gap, not proof the registers do not survive. For these, consult the repositories below.
- **Language:** English.

### Closing the church-register gap: repositories and indexes
Because `collections_search` and `catalog_search` returned **zero** matches for Billy parish specifically, the following named repositories and indexes (drawn from the Ireland Church Records wiki page) are where the Catholic/Presbyterian/Church of Ireland registers for this parish, or substitute indexes to them, are most likely to be found or searched:

- **Public Record Office of Northern Ireland (PRONI)** — 2 Titanic Boulevard, Titanic Quarter, Belfast, BT3 9HQ, Northern Ireland. Tel: 028 9053 4800. Email: proni@communities-ni.gov.uk. PRONI's "Guide to Church Records" (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/sites/default/files/publications/Guide-to-Church-Records-October-2019.pdf) identifies which churches existed in each Northern Ireland parish, what registers survive, and whether PRONI holds them on microfilm or as originals; PRONI also lists "Digitised Church Records Available in PRONI" (https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/digitised-church-records-available-proni#toc-1). General enquiries: https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/proni-enquiry-service.
- **Church of Ireland RCB Library** — Braemor Park, Churchtown, Dublin 14, D14 N735. Tel: +353 (0)1 492 3979. Email: library@ireland.anglican.org. Holds and can search Church of Ireland parish registers (https://store.ireland.anglican.org/genealogy); its "List of Parish Registers" PDF (https://www.ireland.anglican.org/cmsfiles/pdf/AboutUs/library/registers/ParishRegisters/PARISHREGISTERS.pdf) states which Church of Ireland registers for a parish survive and where held — useful given that two-thirds of Church of Ireland registers nationally were destroyed in 1922.
- **National Library of Ireland — Catholic parish register microfilms**, searchable free online at https://registers.nli.ie/. Covers Catholic baptism/marriage registers by parish/diocese.
- **RootsIreland** — http://www.rootsireland.ie/, a paid index covering many Irish civil and church parish registers by county, including Antrim.
- **IrishGenealogy.ie** — https://www.irishgenealogy.ie/en/ (coverage noted by the Wiki as County Kerry, western/northwestern County Cork, and most of Dublin city — **not** confirmed to cover County Antrim, so do not rely on it for Billy without checking).
- **FindMyPast** — subscription indexes specifically named by the Wiki: "Irish Parish Register Baptisms & Confirmations, Ffolliott Collection" (https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/irish-parish-register-baptisms-and-confirmations-ffolliott-collection), the companion Marriages and Burials Ffolliott indexes, "Ireland Roman Catholic Parish Marriages" (https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/ireland-roman-catholic-parish-marriages), and the Non-Conformist births/baptisms, burials, congregational-records and marriages indexes (e.g. https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-Records/ireland-non-conformist-births-and-baptisms) — relevant given the Presbyterian/Covenanter/Methodist presence in Billy.
- **Ancestry** — "Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1655–1915" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/61039/) and "Ireland, Abstracts of Wills and Marriages, 1620–1923" (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/62059), both index & images, subscription.
- **FamilySearch** — "Ireland, Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage License Bonds Indexes, 1623-1866" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/3460239), free index & images, plus "Index to Church of Ireland diocesan marriage licenses, 1630-1845" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/search/catalog/217297, index only).
- **Ulster Historical Foundation** — http://www.ancestryireland.com/?ai_home/ — a large Ulster-specific database covering multiple Antrim parishes and record types.
- **Substitutes for lost/unindexed originals:** the Betham, Crossle, and Thrift Genealogical Abstracts at FindMyPast (https://search.findmypast.com/search-world-records/betham-genealogical-abstracts, .../crossle-genealogical-abstracts, .../thrift-genealogical-abstracts) were compiled before the 1922 Public Record Office fire and can stand in where originals were destroyed.
(All of the above are cited from https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Church_Records, which this survey fetched directly.)

### Census records
- No Irish census returns survive for 1780–1870 generally (the pre-1901 Irish censuses were destroyed); this survey did not confirm specific Antrim detail — the `collections_search`, `catalog_search` and county-level wiki pages for Billy/Antrim returned no census-specific content. Treat the 19th-century Irish census gap as background knowledge, not something this survey verified for Billy.
- **Substitutes identified:** Griffith's Valuation (started by Richard Griffith in the 1840s) and Tithe Applotment records (beginning in the 1820s) are named by the Billy parish page as the main pre-census substitutes for this parish. (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Billy_Civil_Parish,_County_Antrim,_Northern_Ireland_Genealogy)

### Probate and court records
- The Billy parish page points only to the general "Ireland Probate Records" article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Probate_Records) with no Billy-specific holdings found by `catalog_search` (0 hits) or `collections_search` (0 results) — a confirmed gap in this survey, not evidence the records don't exist.
- The Ireland, Indexes to Wills, Probate Administration, Marriage Bonds and Licences, 1591-1866 index at Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/62077/) is a named substitute/finding aid.

### Land records
- Tax/valuation records for the parish were located: "Valuation" records for Ballylinny (within Billy), **1867–1881**, catalogued as VAL 12B/1/7B, 76 images, browse-only (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — image group 004689599 (from `volume_search`). This set runs just past 1870 but is the only land/tax-adjacent volume this survey found specific to the parish.
- General guidance: see https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Land_and_Property, as referenced on the Billy parish page.

### Military records
- No Billy-specific military records were returned by `catalog_search` or `volume_search`. General Ireland guidance only: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Military_Records (link present in the Ireland Church Records page's navigation panel, not separately fetched in this survey — treat as unconfirmed detail).

### Cemetery records
- Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) was returned by `external_links_search` as a general cemetery-records resource; no Billy-specific cemetery listing was confirmed in this survey.

### Newspaper records
- Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) was returned generically by `external_links_search`; no Billy- or Antrim-specific title or date range was confirmed.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not surveyed in parish-specific detail; general Ireland emigration guidance exists at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Emigration_and_Immigration (named in the Ireland Church Records navigation panel but not independently fetched).

### School records
- A digitized volume was found: "Deffrick National School Girls," V. 239-240, covering Billy parish, **1 Apr 1867 – 11 Sep 1933**, 50 images, **0% indexed, not full-text searchable (browse-only)** — image group 008682995_005_M94W-68Y. This runs past 1870 but overlaps the tail of the target period.

### Tax records
- See Land records above (Griffith's Valuation from the 1840s; Tithe Applotments from the 1820s; the VAL 12B/1/7B volume 1867–1881).

- An indexed collection titled **"Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records"** (1708–1985, ~982,415 persons) also appears in FamilySearch collections.

### Probate Records
- A FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber **004812990**, 286 images) covers **Probate Records, 1845–1880** — only 4% name-indexed, but **full-text searchable**.

## Boundary changes

### Probate and court records
- `volume_search` volume imageGroupNumber **004812990**, 286 images, Probate Records, 1845–1880 — only 4% name-indexed but full-text searchable (flagged as full-text searchable, not name-indexed).

### Other record types

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Federal census 1850–1860 (imageGroupNumber 007621224, indexed); Probate Records 1845–1880 (imageGroupNumber 004812990, full-text searchable only); Lutheran Church Records 1840–1875 (imageGroupNumber 004288771, browse-only); "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" (id SYNTH-PA-CHURCH); "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994" (id 1999196) | Covers census, probate, and one denomination's church records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 3 digitized volumes total for this place and period (`totalResults: 3`, `complete: true`), and all three are detailed above — this is the complete matched set, not a partial page.

### Physical repositories

## Known record losses

## Research tips

- The 1850–1860 federal census (imageGroupNumber 007621224) is 96% indexed — start there before the browse-only church register.

- The probate volume (imageGroupNumber 004812990) is full-text searchable even though only 4% name-indexed — use full-text search rather than assuming it is unsearchable.
- `place_population` and `catalog_search` returned no data for this place this run; re-querying later, or checking the FamilySearch Catalog manually, may surface more.
- Consider widening to the Pennsylvania state level for land, military, and naturalization records, since none were found at the county level this run.

Because no project path was supplied, this guide was not saved to a project; nothing further was persisted.

---
This survey covered Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania for roughly the 1840s through 1860s. It found that the 1850 and 1860 federal census records for the county are well indexed and searchable online through FamilySearch, that a Lutheran congregation's baptism, marriage, and burial register from 1840–1875 survives but can only be browsed page by page (with some entries in German) since it has no name index, and that a probate (wills and estate) volume from 1845–1880 can be searched by keyword even though it isn't indexed by name. Several important record types — land deeds, military records, cemetery and newspaper records, and information about physical archives or courthouses holding original paper records — could not be confirmed in this search and should be treated as open gaps rather than as records that don't exist, and the usual FamilySearch background pages that normally describe a place's specific record history returned only generic, non-Schuylkill content this time, so dates like when official birth, marriage, and death registration began could not be confirmed. The next step would be to re-run or supplement this search against the county-level and Pennsylvania state archives directly, and to check courthouse and historical-society holdings for the land, military, cemetery, and newspaper records this survey could not confirm.

## Christ Church, Philadelphia — Original 1734 Marriage Register

**Short answer:** The original register is almost certainly held by the parish itself; no digitized copy turned up in this survey.

---

### Jurisdiction context
Christ Church (founded 1695) was the premier Anglican parish in colonial Philadelphia. In 1734 it sat in the Province of Pennsylvania; Pennsylvania County boundaries have been stable since 1682, so there are no jurisdiction complications here.

---

### Where the original is held

| Custodian | Why | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Christ Church, Philadelphia (the parish)** | An active congregation normally retains its own original registers — the FamilySearch Research Wiki states that for still-active parishes, the church itself is the custodian, not the diocese | Contact the church directly |
| **Diocese of Pennsylvania** | Holds records only for *closed* Episcopal parishes in the region — Christ Church is still active, so the Diocese is not applicable here | N/A |

**What to do:** Contact Christ Church in Philadelphia directly and ask to view or receive a copy of its original 1734 marriage register. The church has an archives program; their staff can tell you viewing policies and appointment procedures.

---

### What *is* available online

The **Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)** holds an abstract/transcription collection — *Pennsylvania, HSP, Marriages (1512–1989)* — indexed on FamilySearch. This can confirm whether a particular marriage entry exists and give you the date and names, but it is a later transcription, not the original volume.

FamilySearch's own catalog and digitized image groups returned **no copy of Christ Church's register** in this survey. That is a cataloging gap, not proof no microfilm exists — a direct inquiry to the FamilySearch Family History Library in Salt Lake City (or a local FamilySearch Center) may turn one up.

---

### Suggested next steps

1. **Contact Christ Church, Philadelphia** to ask about access to its 1734 marriage register.
2. Search the FamilySearch HSP Marriages collection first to confirm the entry and get the exact date before you request the original.
3. Call or email the **FamilySearch Family History Library** to ask whether a microfilm of Christ Church's early registers was made — the Wiki notes many Pennsylvania Episcopal parishes were filmed, and a zero result in an automated catalog search does not rule that out.
4. If the parish cannot accommodate in-person viewing, ask whether the **Diocese of Pennsylvania** holds reference microfilm or photocopies for research use, even for active parishes.

---

*Note: No tool result in this survey returned a specific street address or contact procedure for Christ Church's archives. Confirm access arrangements with the parish before visiting.*

# Locality Guide: Christ Church, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1734)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia was founded in 1682; Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania has existed since that date (`place_search`: "Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States", dateRange +1682/).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of Pennsylvania (colonial, in 1734); now Pennsylvania, United States.
- **Religious context:** Christ Church, founded 1695, is the historic Anglican/Episcopal parish of colonial Philadelphia and remains an active congregation today.
- **Key point for this request:** Christ Church is still an active Episcopal parish. Per the FamilySearch Wiki page on Pennsylvania Church Records, "for parishes that remain active, contact the church directly for access to its original registers" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records). The Diocese of Pennsylvania (also in Philadelphia) holds records only for **closed** Episcopal churches in Bucks, Chester, Delaware, Montgomery, and Philadelphia counties — not for a parish still operating, so the Diocese is not the custodian of Christ Church's own 1734 register.

## Boundary changes
Philadelphia's county boundaries have been stable since 1682; no jurisdictional split affects this parish or period.

## Available record types

### Church records
- **Denomination:** Anglican/Church of England in 1734; Protestant Episcopal after 1789. Record types: baptisms, marriages, burials.
- **Where the originals are:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki, an active parish's own original registers are held by the parish itself, not by the diocese or a historical society — so for Christ Church specifically, the original 1734 marriage register should be sought through the church (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records). No tool result in this survey named a specific archive address or reading-room procedure for Christ Church's own records; that must be confirmed directly with the parish/archives.
- **Derivative holdings found (not originals):** The Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) in Philadelphia holds a FamilySearch-indexed collection, "Pennsylvania, HSP, Marriages (1512–1989)," among three related HSP collections — but the Wiki page explicitly describes these as **abstracts taken from various Pennsylvania church records**, not the registers themselves (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records). This is useful for finding a transcribed entry, but it is not the original volume you asked about and cannot substitute for it.
- **Catalog search result:** A FamilySearch Catalog search for "Christ Church" and for "Christ Church marriage register" against Philadelphia returned zero hits in this survey (`catalog_search`, totalHits: 0). That is a cataloguing gap, not evidence the records don't exist — FamilySearch's own microfilming program did reach many Pennsylvania Episcopal parishes, but no matching entry surfaced here.

### Vital records (civil registration)
Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration in 1734; statewide registration began in 1906 (deaths) and 1913 (births/marriages) per the FamilySearch Wiki research-strategies page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Research_Strategies). For 1734, church registers like Christ Church's are the primary record, not a substitute.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Pennsylvania, HSP, Marriages (1512–1989) — abstracts from various PA church records | Gives a transcribed/indexed version of marriage entries, not the original image | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` for Pennsylvania 1700–1750 returned only 3 digitized volumes, none of them Episcopal church registers (probate, death, and naturalization volumes) — Christ Church's own register was not found among FamilySearch's digitized image groups in this survey.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Christ Church, Philadelphia (the parish itself) | Likely custodian of its own original registers, as an active congregation | Contact the church directly — no tool result in this survey gave a specific contact/access procedure |
| Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia | Abstracts/transcriptions of PA church records (marriages, births/baptisms, deaths/burials, congregational records) | In-person research library |
| Diocese of Pennsylvania (Philadelphia) | Records of **closed** Episcopal parishes only — not applicable to Christ Church, which is active | N/A for this request |

## Records NOT online
The original Christ Church marriage register itself was not found in any online database in this survey (FamilySearch collections, volumes, or catalog). Only a derivative abstract collection (HSP Marriages) surfaced.

## Known record losses
No tool result in this survey reported any loss or destruction of Christ Church's registers. Nothing here suggests the originals do not survive — only that this survey could not confirm their current physical location beyond "the parish, if active" per the Wiki's general rule.

## Research tips
- Because Christ Church is described by the FamilySearch Wiki as an active parish, go to the source: contact Christ Church, Philadelphia directly to ask about access to its original 1734 marriage register (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records).
- Use the Historical Society of Pennsylvania's "Marriages (1512–1989)" collection on FamilySearch to find a transcribed entry first — it may confirm the marriage exists and give you the right date/names before you request to see the original.
- If the parish cannot provide access, ask the Diocese of Pennsylvania whether it holds microfilm or photocopies for research purposes, even though its stated holdings are for closed parishes — dioceses sometimes also hold reference copies of active parishes' early registers.
- Check the FamilySearch Library (Salt Lake City) and local FamilySearch Centers for a microfilm copy, which the Wiki notes exists for many Pennsylvania church records.
- A zero result in the FamilySearch Catalog for "Christ Church" is a cataloguing gap in this survey, not proof the register was never filmed — a research trip or call to the FamilySearch Library, or a direct catalog search done differently, could still turn one up.

# Locality Guide: Alabama region, pre-statehood (Mississippi Territory / Alabama Territory, c. 1798–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The present state of Alabama did not exist in 1800. The region was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (established 1798), which covered both present-day Alabama and Mississippi. The eastern portion was reorganized as the **Alabama Territory** in 1817, becoming the State of Alabama in 1819.

**Earlier claims:** Before 1798 the area was contested among France, Britain, and Spain, with early European settlement around Mobile Bay (French, 1702). Spain continued to claim the Gulf Coast strip (including Mobile) until 1813.

**Key context:** Significant Euro-American settlement followed the Creek War of 1813–1814; the Creek and Cherokee nations held much of the interior through this period, which affects what civil/county records exist for the earliest years.

---

## Boundary Changes

| Period | Jurisdiction |
|---|---|
| Before 1798 | French/British/Spanish-claimed territory |
| 1798–1817 | Mississippi Territory |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory (split from Mississippi Territory) |
| 1819 onward | State of Alabama |

**Research tip:** Treat these as one continuous record trail under three successive jurisdictional names — search for the same place under all three.

---

## Confirmed Record Types & Holdings

### Land Records
- **FamilySearch:** "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (collection ID 1919694, 312,450 people) — directly covers the target period
- **Browse-only volume:** Image group **004498712**, 143 images, "Territorial land and court records," 1799–1817, for Mississippi Territory — **not name-indexed, not full-text searchable; browse image-by-image only**
- Federal land distributed via General Land Office under Mississippi Territory land districts

### Court Records
- **FamilySearch:** "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920" (collection ID 1855293, 245,670 people)
- Same browse-only volume (004498712, 1799–1817) also covers court records

### Census / Census Substitutes
- **FamilySearch:** "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (collection ID 1927171, 198,340 people) — these are *substitute* records (tax lists, territorial censuses), not original federal schedules; treat accordingly

### Church Records
- **FamilySearch:** "Mississippi, Church Records, 1800-1950" (collection ID 2034891, 87,654 people)
- Early Mobile Bay Catholic records likely predate this (French/Spanish origins, 1702+)
- Protestant denominations spread with American settlers post-1813

### Vital Records
- No civil registration existed at the territorial level for this period; church registers and county court records are the substitutes

### Military
- No Mississippi Territory- or Alabama-specific military collection was returned. NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) holds federal-level service, pension, and bounty-land records

### Cemetery / Newspapers / Immigration
- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) — general coverage
- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — general archive; no territory-specific titles confirmed
- Mobile was an active early port; no port manifests for this period were confirmed online

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What it holds for this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Land records 1798–1907; county court records 1799–1920; census substitutes 1792–1890; church records 1800–1950; browse-only territorial volume 1799–1817 | Free |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal land patents, early naturalization, military records | Free (online finding aids) |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census collection | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History** | Successor state archive for Alabama records | Unconfirmed by tool — check directly |
| **Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History** | Successor state archive for Mississippi Territory records | Unconfirmed by tool — check directly |

---

## Known Gaps in This Survey
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages for this jurisdiction returned only generic fallback content — no place-specific guidance was retrievable. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki site directly at [www.familysearch.org/wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/wiki) for the Mississippi Territory and Alabama pages
- `catalog_search` returned zero hits for both "Mississippi Territory" and "Alabama" — a cataloging gap, not proof the catalog holds nothing; check NARA directly
- No confirmed physical repository holdings (county courthouse, state archive) were returned by tools; the Alabama and Mississippi state archives are standard practice but not confirmed by a tool result in this session

## Research Strategy

1. **Search all three jurisdictional names** — Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), Alabama Territory (1817–1819), and Alabama state/county records (1819+) — as one continuous trail
2. **Start with the confirmed FamilySearch collections** — prioritize the territorial land records (1919694) and county court records (1855293), as land and court records are the strongest confirmed category for this period

5. **Consult the Alabama and Mississippi state archives** directly — they are the logical holders of original county and territorial records not yet digitized

# Locality Guide: Ohio, United States (circa 1790, pre-statehood / Northwest Territory era)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** The area was part of the Northwest Territory, established under the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio did not become a separate state until 1803. FamilySearch's own place record dates "Ohio, United States" from `+1803/`, meaning for 1790 the governing jurisdiction is the **Northwest Territory**, not the state.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory of the United States (1787–1803), successor to earlier claims by Virginia and Connecticut, whose land-grant systems (Virginia Military District, Connecticut Western Reserve) created distinct, separately administered tracts.
- **Early population:** Sparse, concentrated at a few early settlements (e.g., Marietta, founded 1788). County organization proceeded progressively — Washington County, organized 1788, is the earliest confirmed in this survey.

---

## Boundary Changes

This is primarily a **temporal jurisdiction shift**, not a geographic split:
- Pre-1787: Unorganized frontier with competing colonial-era claims (Virginia, Connecticut).
- 1787–1803: Northwest Territory — records were created under territorial and county-level authority.
- 1803: Ohio statehood — FamilySearch's hierarchy dates "Ohio" only from this point.

**Practical rule:** For 1790 research, search under "Northwest Territory" *and* the specific county (e.g., Washington County) rather than "Ohio" alone. Searches scoped only to "Ohio" may miss records correctly filed under the territory.

Additionally, land records in this era fell under **separate grant systems**:
- **Virginia Military District** (metes and bounds surveying)
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** (distinct granting authority)

Which system applies depends on the exact location of your ancestor's land.

---

## Available Records & Gaps

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No confirmed statewide vital registration** for 1790 was found in this survey.
- **County marriages:** "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (FamilySearch collection, 3,047,356 people) overlaps the target period.
- **Births/Deaths:** No confirmed births or deaths collection reaches back to 1790; the death collection found begins only in 1840.
- **Gap substitute:** Church records are the primary alternative for births and deaths in this period.

### Church Records
- "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (FamilySearch, 678,234 people) directly covers 1790.
- Language: English.
- Specific denominations or settlements represented could not be confirmed in this survey.

### Census Records
- **No federal census** covered the Northwest Territory in 1790 as a state enumeration.
- **Substitute:** County tax lists are the best-confirmed census substitute for pre-statehood Ohio (see Tax Records below).

### Land Records
- **Browse-only territorial volume:** Image group 005112233, "Territorial Land Records," Northwest Territory, 1788–1799, 51 images — **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed page by page.**
- **Indexed collection:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840" (FamilySearch, 234,567 people).
- **Identify the tract first** (Virginia Military District vs. Connecticut Western Reserve) before searching, as the granting authority differs.

### Tax Records
- Washington County tax volume (image group 005112240), 1799–1803, 73 images, 12% name-indexed — mostly browse-only.
- "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850" (FamilySearch, 345,890 people) begins in 1800.
- These are the **best confirmed substitutes for a pre-statehood census**.

### Probate & Court Records
- No Ohio-specific digitized probate or court records from this period were returned; county courthouse-level holdings are the expected location, but were not confirmed in this survey.

### Military Records
- Not surveyed with specificity; the period borders the post-Revolutionary War bounty-land era. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) are general resources.

### Cemetery Records
- No Ohio-specific burial-register data was returned; Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a general resource.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What's available for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County marriages (1789+), church records (1787+), land records (1787+), tax records (1800+), territorial land browse volume (1788–1799) | Free |

Here is the locality guide produced for California during the Gold Rush era:

---

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1860)

## Jurisdiction Overview
California was admitted as a state in 1850, bypassing territorial status. Following the discovery of gold at Sutter's Mill in January 1848, roughly 300,000 people migrated to California from across the U.S. and abroad, producing a transient, predominantly male population from diverse origins.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **California, County Marriages, 1850–1952** — ~1.1 million people, indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1452832)
- **California, County Births, 1850–1919** — ~789,000 people, indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2017276)
- These are **county-level** civil records; a statewide registration system had not yet been established. No indexed death records for this period were found.

### Census Records
- **California State Census, 1850–1852** — volume imageGroupNumber 006601001, 522 images, 88% name-indexed and full-text searchable. Critically useful because the 1850 federal census famously **undercounted the itinerant mining population**.
- **Federal Census:** 1850 and 1860 federal censuses apply; search these through FamilySearch or Ancestry directly.

### Mining and Occupational Records
- **Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855** — imageGroupNumber 006601002, 340 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**. Must be paged through manually but can place a miner at a specific camp and date.

### Immigration / Arrival Records
- **Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** — imageGroupNumber 006601003, 298 images, **0% indexed, browse-only**. Many Gold Rush migrants arrived by ship (around Cape Horn or via Panama); also check NARA passenger-list holdings for San Francisco arrivals.

### Voter / Residency Records
- **California, Great Registers, 1866–1910** — ~1.3 million people, indexed on FamilySearch (collection 1923340). Just after this period but the nearest large identity record for California residents once registration begins.

### Church Records (Pre-Statehood)
- **California, Mission Records, 1769–1850** — ~98,000 people, FamilySearch (collection 1804372). Useful primarily for Californio families already present before statehood, not later Gold Rush arrivals.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County births/marriages, state census, mining registers, port arrivals, mission records | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Local newspaper notices | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, land patents, military | Free/in-person |

---

## Browse-Only (No Name Index)
Two key record sets are digitized but **not searchable by name** — plan for image-by-image review:
- Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855
- Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858

---

## Research Tips
1. **Use the 1850–1852 California State Census** to find miners missed by the 1850 federal census.
2. **Mining claim registers** can place a person at a specific district and date even when no vital record survives — worth the browse effort.
3. **Check full passenger manifests**, not just presumed heads of household — women and children were often listed.
4. **Pre-1906 naturalizations** could be filed in any court of record; start with county courthouses (San Francisco's 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed many municipal records).
5. As many as **14 total digitized volumes** for this place/period exist on FamilySearch; only 3 were detailed in this survey — a focused catalog search by county or mining district may surface more.

---

## Coverage Gaps in This Survey
- No California-specific land record details were confirmed (check the BLM General Land Office site for land patents).
- FamilySearch's dedicated California wiki pages returned only generic template content rather than place-specific guidance, so some categories (land, newspapers, physical archives) could not be fully confirmed.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700s Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction Overview
- **Origin:** New York City began as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam (1624), seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York. It served as capital of the Province of New York.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (colonial); New York became a U.S. state in 1788.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian churches were the primary congregations and kept the most extensive records.

---

## Available Record Types

### Church Records *(primary substitute for civil vital records in this era)*
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776** — Available on FamilySearch as digitized images (image group **007733180**, 211 images). **Important caveats:** 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, must be browsed page by page, and written entirely in **Dutch**.
- **"New York, Church Records, 1640–1940"** (FamilySearch collection id 1469062, ~2.3M persons) — An aggregated multi-denomination collection covering the colonial period, useful for Anglican and Presbyterian records as well.

### Probate Records
- **"New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971"** (FamilySearch collection id 1542780) — Covers wills, inventories, and estate administrations through the full 1700s.

### Land Records
- **"New York, Land Records, 1630–1975"** (FamilySearch collection id 2078654) — Deeds, grants, and patents from the colonial period forward.

### Tax Records
- **"New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804"** (FamilySearch collection id 1678432) — Falls at the tail end of the period; useful as a population/household substitute since no colonial census exists.

### Census Records
- **None for most of this period.** The first U.S. federal census was 1790 — right at the end of this window. No colonial-era provincial census was confirmed. Use tax and land records as substitutes.

### Military Records
- Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) and NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) are the general repositories for colonial militia and Revolutionary War service. No New York City-specific colonial military collection was confirmed by this survey.

### Newspaper Records
- Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) covers historical titles generally; no specific colonial New York City title or date range was confirmed.

### Cemetery/Burial Records
- Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) as a general resource. Church burial registers would fall under the church records above.

### Immigration / Naturalization
- New York City was a major colonial port. Colonial-era passenger and naturalization records would be held at NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); no specific collection was confirmed for this period.

---

## Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Church records, probate, land records, tax rolls, Dutch Reformed image volume | Free |
| Fold3 | Military service/pension records | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census from 1790 onward | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspaper archives | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal military, immigration/naturalization | Free |

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **The Dutch Reformed register (image group 007733180)** is entirely in Dutch and must be browsed image by image — plan to read Dutch or use a translator, and search by date range rather than name.
2. **No federal census before 1790** — use the tax assessment rolls and land/probate records as household substitutes.
3. **Search the aggregate church records collection** (id 1469062) alongside the Dutch Reformed volume to catch Anglican and Presbyterian baptisms, marriages, and burials.
4. **Probate + land records together** often name the same family members and can substitute for missing vital records in this era.
5. **FamilySearch's catalog** returned zero results for New York City in this search — that is likely a cataloguing gap, not proof records don't exist. Check directly with the relevant municipal and denominational archives for physical holdings.
6. **The FamilySearch Research Wiki** pages for New York City returned only generic boilerplate during this survey — worth consulting directly at familysearch.org/wiki for more New York-specific guidance.

---

The core strategy for colonial New York City is: start with church registers (especially the Dutch Reformed volume and the aggregate church records collection), then corroborate with probate and land records, and use tax rolls as a population substitute for the pre-1790 period.

# Locality Guide: New York City, New York (1700-1800, British Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New York City dates to 1624 as the Dutch colony of New Amsterdam; seized by the English in 1664 and renamed New York (per Wikipedia). It served as capital of the Province of New York and briefly as the first U.S. capital.
- **County seat / administrative center:** New York City itself was the colonial and provincial center.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Province of New York (colonial); New York, United States (`standardPlace`: "New York, United States", dateRange from 1788 per `place_search`).
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for "New York, New York, United States" for 1700-1800 — this survey could not confirm population figures from that tool.
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and administrative center (Wikipedia).
- **Ethnic composition:** Dutch, English, and other European settlers; Dutch Reformed congregation is documented through a dedicated record set (see Church records).
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian churches kept extensive records (Wikipedia).
- **Key historical events:** British colonial rule throughout the 1700s; the city functioned as capital of New York Province.

## Boundary changes
New York became a state in 1788 (per `place_search`'s dateRange for "New York, United States"); before that it was the Province of New York under British rule. This survey found no record of New York City's own boundaries changing within the 1700-1800 window; treat the colonial-era and early-state-era record series as a continuous trail for the city.

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **What exists / Pre-registration alternatives:** For the 1700s, church registers are the practical substitute for civil vital records (see Church records below); this is consistent with the generic Wiki guidance that church records "often predate civil registration by decades or centuries," though that page is not New York-specific.
- **Gaps:** No statewide civil registration data confirmed for this period by any tool in this survey.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Dutch Reformed, Anglican, and Presbyterian (Wikipedia).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials.
- **Where held:** `volume_search` found one digitized volume: image group **007733180**, 211 images, covering "Dutch Reformed Church Registers," New York City, 1700-1776. It is **0% name-indexed** and **not full-text searchable** — browse-only, image by image — and is in **Dutch (language code "nl")**, so the researcher must read Dutch to use it directly. `collections_search` also lists **"New York, Church Records, 1640-1940"** (collection id 1469062, ~2,345,678 persons), which overlaps the colonial period and spans multiple denominations.
- **Gaps:** This survey found no distinct Anglican or Presbyterian register set named by any tool beyond the aggregate "Church Records" collection — report this as a coverage gap in what was specifically confirmed, not evidence those registers don't exist.
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed registers for this period are in Dutch.

### Census records

- **State/provincial census:** No colonial-era New York census was identified by any tool in this survey.
- **Access:** Not applicable for most of the period; see Tax records below as a substitute.

### Probate and court records

# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775–1783, Revolutionary War focus)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; statehood dates from 1788, so the Revolutionary years (1775–1783) are pre-statehood — no county-level breakdown tool data was returned for this period.
- **Key historical events:** Virginia contributed more troops to the Revolutionary War than any other colony/state, and major campaigns (including the Yorktown siege, 1781) were fought on Virginia soil.
- **Record-keeping tradition:** Virginia kept county-level records from the 1630s, giving it one of the best-documented colonial record bases in British North America — most Revolutionary-era personal records (land, probate, court) will be found at the *county*, not state, level.

## Boundary changes
Virginia had dozens of counties by 1775, and many were subdivided repeatedly through the colonial and early national periods. Because ancestors may be recorded under a county that no longer exists or whose boundaries shifted, identify the specific county of residence before searching, and check that county's formation history.

---

## Available Record Types

### Military Records (State Level — Revolutionary War)
- **What exists:** A dedicated FamilySearch collection, **"Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783"** (collection id 1945678, ~345,678 person entries) directly matches the target period.
- **Bounty land:** A browse-only digitized volume of **"Revolutionary War land bounty warrants" for Virginia, 1779–1800** (image group 005301447, 341 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) must be browsed image by image.
- **Where held:** Service records, pension files, and bounty-land warrants are generally at the National Archives (NARA); **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) is a curated military-records resource. Virginia's own adjutant general/militia records would be at the **Library of Virginia** — unconfirmed by a tool in this run; treat as a lead to verify.

### Land Records
- **"Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900"** (id 1734285, ~2.57 million entries) overlaps the Revolutionary period.
- Revolutionary soldiers and their heirs frequently redeemed bounty-land warrants for land grants — search the bounty-warrant volume (005301447) alongside ordinary land-grant/deed records.
- County courthouses held the original deed books; for warrant-based grants, see state land office records.

### Probate and Court Records
- **"Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920"** (id 2134567, ~1.79 million entries) and the Land/Marriage/Will collection both span 1775–1783.
- **Digitized example:** Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795 (image group 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed) — directly relevant and partially searchable.
- County court order books recorded wartime business — oaths of allegiance, impressment of supplies, militia appointments — that can place a man in a specific county at a specific date even without a formal military record.

### Tax Records
- **"Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850"** (id 1456723, ~456,789 entries) begins right at the war's end; a full-text-searchable **"State enumerations / tax lists"** volume for Virginia, 1782–1799 (image group 005301449, 87 images) covers the immediate post-war transition.
- No federal census exists before 1790. Personal-property and tithable tax lists are the main substitute for enumerating who lived where during the war years themselves (1775–1781), since they predate the surviving tax series' 1782 start.

### Church Records
- **"Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929"** (id 1598230, ~1.23 million entries) covers the period.
- The established church in colonial Virginia was Anglican (Church of England), with vestries that also administered local poor relief — vestry books can name militia-aged men and their households.

### Census Records
No federal census exists before 1790, and no surviving 1790 Virginia schedule was confirmed. Use tax lists and militia/muster records as the substitute for 1775–1783.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for This Place | Gap It Fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Military Records 1775-1783 (id 1945678); Land/Marriage/Will 1600-1900 (id 1734285); County Court Records 1650-1920 (id 2134567); Tax Records 1782-1850 (id 1456723); Church Records 1680-1929 (id 1598230); volumes 005301447, 005301448, 005301449 | Military service/bounty land, county court, tax, land, church | Free |
| Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ | Military service and pension records at NARA | Subscription |
| Ancestry | https://www.ancestry.com/ | Post-1790 census collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | https://www.findagrave.com/ | Cemetery/burial records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | https://www.newspapers.com/ | Historical newspapers (wartime notices, obituaries) | Subscription |
| National Archives (NARA) | https://www.archives.gov/ | Original military service and pension files | Free (in person) / some digitized |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia *(unconfirmed by tool — verify directly)* | Likely holder of state militia/adjutant-general records and county records transferred from courthouses | In-person or written request |
| County courthouse (specific county TBD) | Original deed, will, and court order books | In-person or by mail |
| National Archives (NARA) | Original Revolutionary War pension and bounty-land application files | In-person at Washington, DC, or ordered copies |

---

## Records Not Online
The bounty-land-warrant volume (005301447) and Augusta County court order books (005301448) are online as digitized images but are **not (or only partially) name-indexed** — they cannot be found by name search and must be browsed image by image. No evidence was found that the Library of Virginia's physical militia or adjutant-general holdings have been digitized.

## Known Record Losses
Several FamilySearch Wiki pages for Virginia (Vital Records, Military Records, etc.) returned only generic boilerplate in this run rather than Virginia-specific content. The Wiki page **"Virginia Military Records"** has sections titled "Revolutionary War" and "Post-War Bounty Lands" at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War — read this page directly, as the automated fetch returned only generic text. No tool result confirmed or denied specific courthouse fires or record destruction during the war; treat any such claim as unconfirmed until checked directly.

---

## Research Tips
1. **Identify the specific county first** — Virginia's record tradition routes nearly everything through the county, not the state.
2. **Read the FamilySearch Wiki directly** at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War for the most detailed record-availability guidance.
3. **Search bounty-land warrants (005301447) and 1782-1850 tax records together** — a warrant proves service; the tax record can place the family in a county afterward.
4. **For partially-indexed court order books** (e.g., Augusta County at 61%, image group 005301448), run a name search first, then browse remaining images for a female ancestor, variant surname spelling, or any entry outside the indexed portion.
5. **Substitute tax lists for the census gap** — there is no surviving federal census for Virginia's 1775–1783 years; tithable lists are the primary enumeration substitute.

---

Virginia's wealth of county-level records from the 1630s onward gives you strong tools for tracing Revolutionary War families. The dedicated military collection on FamilySearch, combined with bounty-land warrants, county court order books, and the 1782 tax series, covers the core of what you'll need. Next steps: identify the specific county of residence, then I can build a research plan or search these records for a named person.

### Land records
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" (id 1734285, ~2.57 million entries), overlapping the Revolutionary period.
- **Content note:** Revolutionary soldiers and their heirs frequently redeemed bounty-land warrants for land grants, so the bounty-warrant volume above (005301447) and ordinary land-grant/deed records should both be checked.
- **Where held:** County courthouses and, for warrant-based grants, state land office records; no GLO-style federal land office applies to Virginia (it was a state, not federal-land, jurisdiction).

### Probate and court records
- **What exists:** "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920" (id 2134567, ~1.79 million entries) and "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900" both span 1775–1783.
- **Digitized example:** `volume_search` found Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795 (image group 005301448, 158 images, 61% name-indexed) — a directly relevant, partially searchable volume for that county.

- **Content value:** County court order books recorded routine wartime business — oaths of allegiance, impressment of supplies, appointments to militia offices — that can place a man in a specific county at a specific date even without a military record naming him.

- **What exists:** "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850" (id 1456723, ~456,789 entries) begins right at the tail of the war; `volume_search` separately found a full-text-searchable "State enumerations / tax lists" volume for Virginia, 1782–1799 (image group 005301449, 87 images, not name-indexed but fulltext searchable).

- **What exists:** "Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929" (id 1598230, ~1.23 million entries) covers the period.

This survey did not retrieve denomination-specific detail confirming which parishes' registers survive for 1775–1783; verify parish-level survival separately.

No federal census exists before 1790, and this survey did not confirm a surviving 1790 Virginia schedule. This is squarely a pre-census-coverage gap for the 1775–1783 window; use tax lists and militia/muster records as the substitute.

Not a strong fit for 1775–1783 given no stable federal naturalization process yet existed; no tool result returned anything specific here, so this section is omitted as inapplicable for this period.

Here is what the locality-guide found for New Orleans in the early 1800s:

---

## New Orleans / Orleans Parish, Louisiana — Locality Guide (c. 1800–1830)

### Disasters and Record Losses

The two great fires of **1788 and 1794** destroyed much of colonial-era New Orleans, and subsequent hurricanes, floods, and yellow-fever epidemics caused further damage. However, specifics on exactly which registers and which years were destroyed could not be confirmed from the FamilySearch Wiki pages reached during this survey — that remains an open research question.

### What Survived and Where to Look

Despite those losses, several important record types are confirmed to exist on FamilySearch for this period:

1. **Louisiana Church Records (1800–1830)** — Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital-record substitutes. FamilySearch holds a collection covering this window.

2. **Louisiana Probate Records (1800–1830)** — Estate files often contain names, relationships, and dates that fill in what vital records miss.

3. **New Orleans Notarial Acts (1803–1820)** — Browse-only microfilm. Louisiana's French civil-law tradition means that property transactions, apprenticeships, manumissions, marriage contracts, and many family-legal matters were handled by **notaries**, not county deed offices. These notarial records are among the richest substitutes for missing vital records and are unlike what researchers expect from other U.S. states.

### Key Point for Researchers

Because Louisiana follows **civil law** (French-law tradition) rather than common law, the typical American county courthouse paper trail largely does not apply. Researchers should prioritize:
- Catholic church registers
- Notarial archives
- Probate court files

A research plan built on this guide would sequence those collections and identify fallback sources for the specific ancestors you are tracing.

# Locality Guide: Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts — 1840s Immigrant Arrivals

## Jurisdiction Overview
Boston is a city in Suffolk County, Massachusetts, established from 1630. During the 1840s, it was one of the most important U.S. ports of entry, especially for Irish immigrants fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850, over a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born.

---

## Primary Immigration Record

### Port of Boston Passenger Lists
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection id 1784312, ~1.2M people) — directly covers the 1840s.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 003345210, 389 images, covering 1840–1850 for the Port of Boston.
  - ⚠️ **Important:** Only **3% name-indexed** but **full-text searchable** — standard name searches will mostly miss it. Use full-text search with name spelling variants, ship names, or keywords.
- **Originals:** Held at the National Archives (NARA); FamilySearch holds the digitized copy.
- **Tip:** Examine the full manifest for every family member — infants and children traveling with parents are listed alongside adults.

---

## Supporting Record Types

### Vital Records
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (id 2061550, ~3.5M people) on FamilySearch.
- Massachusetts recorded vital events at the town level historically. The exact start date for civil registration in this period could **not be confirmed** from FamilySearch Wiki pages (they returned generic placeholder content rather than Massachusetts-specific text); verify this detail separately.

### Church Records
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (id 1921657, ~988K people) on FamilySearch.
- Given the heavily Irish Catholic immigrant population, Catholic parish registers are especially relevant. The Archdiocese of Boston Archives holds original sacramental registers; access is by written request.

### Naturalization Records
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790-1906" (id 1459213, ~346K people) on FamilySearch.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in *any* court of record — search this collection broadly, not just for Boston courts.

### Probate Records
- **Collection:** "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (id 1678901, ~568K people) on FamilySearch.

### Census Records
- The **1850 federal census** is the first to list every household member by name — it will capture 1840s arrivals still residing in Boston in 1850, and provides valuable household context passenger lists lack.

### Newspapers
- ***The Pilot*** (Irish Catholic newspaper, Boston) is noted by Wikipedia as having published arrival notices and missing-persons advertisements for 1840s Irish immigrants. No digitized collection was confirmed by tools in this survey; check availability through the Boston Public Library or NARA.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Passenger lists, vital records, church records, naturalization, probate | Free |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Original Port of Boston customs passenger lists; naturalization case files | Free (in-person or request) |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** | State-level vital, court, and naturalization records | In-person or written request |
| **Suffolk County Courthouse** | Local probate and court records | In-person |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish sacramental registers | Written request |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census collections | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Period newspaper articles/notices | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free |

---

## Known Record Gaps
- The Port of Boston passenger list volume for 1840–1850 is only 3% name-indexed; most images must be found via full-text search.
- Physical naturalization case files beyond the index, original church registers, and original courthouse probate files were not reported as fully digitized.
- No specific record losses (fire, flood, etc.) for Boston/Suffolk County were identified in this survey.

---

## Recommended Next Steps
1. **Search the Port of Boston passenger list** (FamilySearch collection 1784312 / volume 003345210) using **full-text search** with name spelling variants — do not rely on the name index alone.
2. **Check the 1850 federal census** for the household after arrival — it provides names, ages, and birthplaces for all family members.
3. **Search Catholic parish registers** via "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" for baptism, marriage, and burial records.
4. **Search naturalization records** broadly across Massachusetts courts using collection id 1459213.
5. **Inquire about *The Pilot*** newspaper at the Boston Public Library or NARA for arrival notices and missing-persons ads.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma / Indian Territory (Mid-1800s, ~1840–1870)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Oklahoma did not exist as a state until 1907. During the mid-1800s, this land was **Indian Territory**, set aside under the Indian Removal Act of 1830 for relocated tribes. The **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — were the dominant groups. Each tribe operated its own government and record-keeping; there was no county or civil court system during this era.

---

## Key Record Types & Collections

### Tribal Rolls and Censuses
- **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (FamilySearch collection id 1987432, ~567,890 people indexed) — overlaps the target period from 1851 onward.
- A digitized volume of **Tribal Enrollment Cards for Indian Territory, 1840–1870** (imageGroupNumber 002298871, ~940 images) is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable on FamilySearch.
- These are the most direct name-level links between an individual and a tribe.

### Land Records
- **"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (FamilySearch collection id 1541872, ~234,567 people) covers the full target window.
- Tribal land was held communally or allotted by treaty — expect allotment and treaty-related documents rather than county deed books.

### Church / Mission Records
- **"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (FamilySearch collection id 1654321) is a key pre-registration alternative. Missionary societies often kept the only baptism, marriage, and burial records before any civil registration existed.

### Civil Vital Records
- **None applicable for this period.** Oklahoma did not begin statewide civil registration until after 1907. The earliest county marriage collection (1890–1995) falls outside the mid-1800s target window.

### Federal / Treaty / Agency Records
- Treaty documents, annuity rolls, and Indian Agency correspondence are **not confirmed online** from this survey. The **National Archives (NARA)** is the likely physical custodian for these materials.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Collections / Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959; Early Land Records 1834–1907; Mission/Church Records 1820–1965; Tribal Enrollment Cards 1840–1870 (images) | Free |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Treaty texts, Indian agency correspondence, annuity payrolls | In-person or online request |
| **Tribal Nation Archives** | Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole — citizenship and enrollment records not digitized elsewhere | Contact each nation's historic preservation office directly |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records | Subscription |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Search by tribal nation, not county** — no county structure existed in Indian Territory during this period.
2. **Start with the rolls** — the FamilySearch "Indian Censuses and Rolls" collection and the 1840–1870 Tribal Enrollment Cards volume are your best first sources for a named individual.
3. **Contact tribal archives directly** — each of the Five Tribes maintains its own genealogy/archive office with citizenship and enrollment records that may not be digitized anywhere else.
4. **Re-search the FamilySearch Catalog by tribal-nation name** — a catalog search by state ("Oklahoma") returned no results in this survey; searching by specific nation name (e.g., "Cherokee Nation") or federal agency name may surface microfilm holdings.
5. **For post-1860s work**, the Dawes Rolls (late 1890s–early 1900s) become the gold standard for tribal citizenship — they predate but feed into later records you may need to work backward from.

---

## Known Gaps in This Survey
- FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma/Indian Territory returned only generic boilerplate rather than tribe-specific guidance; re-check the Wiki directly by hand for more detailed overviews.
- Treaty texts and annuity payrolls were not found in any digitized online collection — treat these as physical-only at NARA until confirmed otherwise.
- Record-loss history (e.g., destruction of specific record series) could not be confirmed from available tools.

---

If you'd like, I can build a **concrete research plan** once you provide a specific family name and which tribal nation you're tracing. I can also help identify the right FamilySearch collections and search strategies for a particular person.

## Jurisdiction overview
