# Locality Guide: Oklahoma, United States (Land Run era, 1889–1907/1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma did not exist as a state until 1907. In 1889, the "Unassigned Lands" opened in the Land Run were part of Indian Territory; in 1890 the area was organized as Oklahoma Territory, separate from the remaining Indian Territory to its east. The Oklahoma_Vital_Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records) states explicitly: "Greer County and No Man's Land, and Unassigned Lands were Indian Territory until April 22, 1889," and that in 1890 "three Judicial Districts were established" in Indian Territory (First District at Muskogee – Cherokee/Creek Nations; Second District at South McAlester – Choctaw Nation; Third District at Ardmore – Seminole/Chickasaw Nations).
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single seat — Oklahoma Territory's counties were organized individually as land was opened; this survey did not confirm individual county seats (none were requested).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States; Indian Territory and (from 1890) Oklahoma Territory were federally administered until the two combined as the State of Oklahoma in 1907.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` returned no data for "Oklahoma, United States" for 1880–1910 — this survey could not confirm population figures for the period.
- **Economy / land use:** The defining event is the April 22, 1889 Land Run opening the "Unassigned Lands" to homestead claims — this directly generated the federal land-entry case files described below.
- **Ethnic composition:** The area was home to Native nations (Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole) in Indian Territory alongside incoming non-Indian settlers after 1889; FamilySearch's "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" collection reflects this.
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by a working wiki page in this survey (see gaps below); FamilySearch's "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" collection (below) indicates mission/church activity in the territory.
- **Key historical events:** The April 22, 1889 Land Run; the 1890 Organic Act splitting the area into Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory; the 1907 merger into statehood.

## Boundary changes
- Before April 22, 1889: the Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory.
- 1890: the Organic Act created Oklahoma Territory (the area opened by the 1889 and later Runs) separate from Indian Territory (still under the Five Civilized Tribes' jurisdictions, with marriages recorded in the three federal Judicial Districts named above).
- 1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged into the State of Oklahoma. Researchers tracing a family through this period should expect records split across territorial, tribal-district, and (after 1907) state/county systems depending on exactly when and where an event occurred — this is a genuine jurisdictional split, not just a renaming, so check all three systems for the relevant years and locale.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Per the Oklahoma_Vital_Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records): births earliest 1891 (county-level, incomplete, "most did not start until after statehood in 1907"); statewide birth and death registration began in 1908, with general compliance by 1928 (90% by 1928 per the page, "generally complied with by 1930" elsewhere on the same page); there was no statewide marriage registration — marriages were recorded at the county level beginning about 1890 "or when the county was created." Before 1890, "no marriages were recorded by the county or state," and from the 1830s to 1889 "very few records exist, some recorded in district courts."
- **What exists:** County marriage bonds/affidavits/licenses from ~1890; FamilySearch's "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (collection 2134789, 913,578 people); "Oklahoma Marriages, 1870-1930" (collection 1681007); "Oklahoma Deaths and Burials, 1864-1941" (collection 3518733).
- **Where held:** County clerk offices for marriages; Oklahoma State Department of Health (statewide, post-1908) for births/deaths; many territorial-era marriages for non-Indian settlers were never recorded locally — some were recorded instead in Arkansas, Kansas, or Texas county courthouses, per the same page.
- **Gaps:** Birth/death records before 1908 are incomplete and county-held only; pre-1890 marriages are largely unrecorded.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, family Bibles, and probate records (the page's own "Alternative Records" list) — see Church records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not confirmed — the Oklahoma_Church_Records page was not fetched in this survey; FamilySearch's "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (collection 1654321, 123,456 people) indicates mission records exist for the territory, mostly reflecting missionary activity among the Five Civilized Tribes rather than settler congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (standard church-record content); not itemized for Oklahoma specifically by any page this survey reached.
- **Where held:** Not confirmed by a working wiki page; FamilySearch's indexed collection above is the only source this survey verified.
- **Language:** Not confirmed.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory were enumerated in the 1900 federal census (statehood came too late for a separate 1890 schedule, and the 1890 federal census is largely destroyed nationwide — this survey did not confirm an Oklahoma-specific substitute).
- **Other enumerations:** FamilySearch's "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (collection 1987432, 567,890 people) — tribal rolls, including Dawes Commission material (see Land records below), are a key substitute/supplement for the 1890s-1900s when no federal census covered the area.
- **Access:** The Indian Censuses and Rolls collection is indexed per `collections_search`; access level for images was not further confirmed in this survey.

### Land records
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Federal — Oklahoma was federal public-domain land opened by Presidential proclamation for the 1889 Run; final patents were issued by the General Land Office (GLO).
- **Types:** `volume_search` found a digitized volume of **Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs** for Oklahoma, 1889-1907 (image group 005221388, 402 images, 74% name-indexed via record search, not full-text searchable). `collections_search` also lists "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (collection 1541872, 234,567 people).
- **Date range:** 1889–1907 for the land-entry case files; 1834–1907 for the Early Land Records collection.
- **Where held:** The GLO homestead case files are a federal record; original case files are held by the U.S. National Archives, with the indexed/digitized version reachable through the identified FamilySearch volume and collection. For patent lookups, the BLM General Land Office website (noted generically in the FamilySearch pages read) is the standard tool, though this survey could not confirm its Oklahoma-specific page.
- **Related tribal land records:** `volume_search` also found "Dawes Commission enrollment jackets," 1898-1910 (image group 005221389, 176 images, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — these document tribal enrollment and allotment, relevant for families with Five Civilized Tribes connections; this volume is **browse-only**, with no name index at all.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships — standard content per the generic FamilySearch guidance read; no Oklahoma-specific probate page was reached in this survey.
- **Where held:** County or district courthouse level (per generic guidance); for events before 1890 in Indian Territory, the relevant court was one of the three federal Judicial Districts named above (Muskogee, South McAlester, Ardmore).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** None specific to the 1889 Run; broader 19th/early 20th century federal military record series (service, pension, draft) are held at NARA per the generic page read; a curated Fold3 link was returned (see Repository guide).

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave was returned by `external_links_search` as a curated resource for Oklahoma.
- **Physical records:** Not confirmed in this survey; sexton/burial-register holdings would need to be checked at individual cemeteries or county historical societies.

### Newspaper records
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com was returned by `external_links_search` as a curated resource; no Oklahoma-specific paper or date range was confirmed in this survey.

### Immigration/emigration records
- Not a primary record type for this inland territory, but note: naturalization petitions for territorial-era settlers could be filed in any court of record, including the federal territorial/Judicial District courts, per the generic U.S. guidance read.

### Tax records
- Not confirmed by any Oklahoma-specific page in this survey; generically, territorial/county tax rolls can substitute for the destroyed or absent 1890 federal census.

### Other record types
- Dawes Commission enrollment records (above) double as a quasi-census/allotment record set critical for any family with claims in or near the Five Civilized Tribes nations bordering the 1889 Run area.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907" (1541872); "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" (1987432); "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890-1995" (2134789); "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965" (1654321); "Oklahoma Marriages, 1870-1930" (1681007); "Oklahoma Deaths and Burials, 1864-1941" (3518733) | County-level marriages from 1890 onward (no statewide marriage registration ever existed); tribal census/roll substitute for missing 1890 federal census; mission/church coverage | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (curated link returned by `external_links_search`) | General federal census coverage | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records (curated link) | Burial/cemetery data not otherwise online | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (curated link) | Obituaries, marriage notices | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (curated link) | Service/pension/draft records | Subscription |
| National Archives (NARA) | archives.gov (curated link) | Original homestead case files and Dawes Commission records | Free (research; copies may have a fee) |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned only 2 digitized volumes for Oklahoma, 1889-1910 (the homestead land-entry case files and the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets) — this is the complete result set for that window, not a partial page. `catalog_search` for "Oklahoma, United States" returned 0 hits, which is a cataloging gap, not evidence that no microfilm/manuscript material exists for the state.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| County clerk offices (by county) | Marriage bonds/licenses from ~1890; early incomplete birth/death records from 1891 | Write/contact the specific county clerk |
| Oklahoma State Department of Health, Vital Records Service (Oklahoma City) | Statewide births/deaths from 1908; delayed birth registrations | Mail/in-person, with eligibility restrictions per state law |
| U.S. National Archives | Original GLO homestead case files; Dawes Commission enrollment jackets | In-person or written request |

## Records NOT online
- Full, unindexed Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (image group 005221389) are online as browse-only page images with 0% name indexing — not searchable by name.
- Pre-1890 marriages for non-Indian settlers were frequently never recorded at all, or recorded across the state line in Arkansas, Kansas, or Texas county courthouses, per the Oklahoma_Vital_Records page — no online index of these exists.
- Birth and death records before 1908 exist only as incomplete county-courthouse holdings, not digitized statewide.

## Known record losses
- No tool result in this survey identified a specific destroyed Oklahoma record series. The incompleteness of pre-1908 vital records reflects the absence of a registration requirement (stated above) rather than a documented loss — this survey found no citation for a courthouse fire or similar loss and does not assert one.

## Research tips
- Because statewide marriage registration never existed in Oklahoma, search at the **county** level from about 1890 onward, and expect many earlier marriages to be unrecorded or recorded across the state line — per the Oklahoma Vital Records page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records).
- For any family present in the 1889 Land Run itself, the federal homestead final-proof case file (image group 005221388, 74% name-indexed) is a primary source — check it before or alongside any state-level vital record, since it predates state registration entirely.
- If the family had any connection to the Five Civilized Tribes or lived near Indian Territory, check the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (image group 005221389) and the "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959" collection — these can substitute for the missing/incomplete early census and vital records.
- Before 1890, route any court-record search for the Indian Territory portion through the correct Judicial District (Muskogee, South McAlester, or Ardmore) rather than a county, since counties did not yet administer those records.
- The FamilySearch Wiki's generic jurisdiction pages (getting-started, online-records, research-tips, and the Oklahoma Land and Property / Territorial Records pages) returned only generic template content in this survey rather than Oklahoma-specific detail — treat these as gaps, not as confirmation that no such records exist, and re-check the live FamilySearch Wiki directly for `Oklahoma Church Records`, `Oklahoma Land and Property`, and `Oklahoma Territorial Records` before concluding on those topics.
- `place_population` returned no data for Oklahoma for this period — population figures for the territory were not confirmed by this survey.

---
This survey covers Oklahoma (as the Oklahoma Territory/Indian Territory area) from about 1880 through 1910, centered on the April 22, 1889 Land Run. The most useful record types are the federal homestead land-entry case files created by the Run itself, county-level marriage records starting around 1890, statewide birth and death records only from 1908 onward, and, for families connected to the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw, or Seminole nations, tribal census rolls and Dawes Commission enrollment files; these are held variously by county clerks, the Oklahoma State Department of Health, and the U.S. National Archives, with indexed copies of several on FamilySearch. The biggest traps are that marriages before 1890 were often not recorded at all or were recorded in a neighboring state, that Indian Territory before 1890 used three separate federal court districts instead of counties, and that the FamilySearch Wiki's detailed Oklahoma-specific pages on church, land, and territorial records could not be confirmed as reached in this pass and should be checked directly. The next step would be to build a research plan around the homestead land-entry file and the relevant county marriage/vital records for the specific family and county in question.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Mississippi Territory, c. 1798–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The land now called Alabama had no separate American civil jurisdiction around 1800. It was organized as the **Mississippi Territory (1798–1817)**, then briefly as the **Alabama Territory (1817–1819)**, before statehood. The Gulf Coast strip around Mobile was administered by Spain as part of West Florida into the early 1810s — records for that area before U.S. annexation may be **Spanish colonial records**, not American territorial ones.

Pre-1819, there were no stable Alabama counties; territorial government for the eastern (Tombigbee/Alabama River) settlements was seated at St. Stephens/Washington County. Settlement came largely from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia, with the Creek and Cherokee nations inhabiting much of the interior. The Creek War (1813–1814) dramatically reshaped settlement patterns just after the period of interest.

---

## Records Found in This Survey

The four FamilySearch collections confirmed as covering this territory and period are:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Date Range | Persons |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records | 1919694 | 1798–1907 | 312,450 |
| Mississippi, County Court Records | 1799–1920 | 1799–1920 | 245,670 |
| Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes | 1927171 | 1792–1890 | 198,340 |
| Mississippi, Church Records | 2034891 | 1800–1950 | 87,654 |

### Land Records
**"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (collection 1919694) opens in the same year the Mississippi Territory was created — this is the primary source for land grants and patents in the region around 1800. Federal rectangular survey applied once U.S. land offices opened. The BLM General Land Office (GLO) website is the conventional source for federal patents, though not independently confirmed for this specific territory in this survey.

### County Court / Probate Records
**"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (collection 1855293) opens in 1799 — directly relevant to the Alabama-region settlements then organized as Mississippi Territory districts. Covers wills, administrations, guardianships, and other civil records filed at the county/district level.

### Census Substitutes (Critical for This Period)
**"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** (collection 1927171) is especially important because the 1800 and 1810 federal census returns for the Alabama area are largely lost. This compiled set — drawing on tax lists, muster rolls, and other enumerations — typically stands in for those missing returns. Its range opens at 1792, well before territorial organization.

### Church Records
**"Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950"** (collection 2034891) opens exactly at 1800 and is the principal substitute for pre-civil-registration vital events (baptisms, marriages, burials). No specific denominations were confirmed for this territory in this survey; expect Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian as the common frontier denominations, but verify.

---

## Browsable / Digitized Volumes — Direct Answer

> **None were found.** A dedicated `volume_search` scoped to "Mississippi Territory, United States" for 1798–1819 returned `totalResults: 0` — no digitized, image-browsable volumes of any kind (indexed, browse-only, or full-text) exist in FamilySearch's volume index for this specific territory and period. This is a genuine gap in digitization coverage, not a partial result.

The FamilySearch Catalog search also returned zero hits when searched at the territory level. A more productive approach may be to search the Catalog by specific **county or district name** (e.g., "Washington County, Mississippi Territory") rather than the territory name as a whole, since the Catalog's place-matching may resolve better at that granularity.

---

## Key Gaps and Research Tips

- **No statewide civil vital registration** existed in this territorial period; church registers and county marriage bonds/licenses are the only substitutes.
- **Spanish colonial records** are essential for the Mobile Bay / Gulf Coast area before U.S. annexation (~1813). These are a separate record universe and were not covered by this survey.
- **Search under all three jurisdiction names** as you trace a family: Mississippi Territory → Alabama Territory → State of Alabama. The same physical location may appear under different names within a single decade depending on the year of a record.
- **Tax lists** are the standard census substitute for lost 1800/1810 returns in this region, but no separate Mississippi Territory tax-list collection was found in this survey; they may appear within collection 1927171 (census substitutes) or as undigitized paper holdings.
- **The Creek War (1813–1814)** generated militia and pension records (at NARA) for men who served in the area — worth checking if your ancestor was present by that date.

# Locality Guide: Mississippi Territory, United States (the Alabama region, c. 1798–1819, before Alabama statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** The area that is now Alabama was not a separate jurisdiction in 1800. `place_search` resolves "Alabama" only as a state with date range beginning 1819. The land was organized as the **Mississippi Territory** (1798–1817, confirmed by `place_search`: "Mississippi Territory, United States", dateRange +1798/1817), and then briefly as the **Alabama Territory** (1817–1819, per Wikipedia) immediately before statehood. Before 1798 and into the early 1800s the southern strip around Mobile was still claimed/administered by Spain (West Florida) rather than the United States.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Not resolvable from the tools used — this period predates organized Alabama counties; territorial government was seated at Natchez and later St. Stephens/Washington County for the eastern (Tombigbee/Alabama) settlements.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** United States (territorial government), with the area claimed at various points by Spain, Britain, France, Georgia, and Native nations (Creek and Cherokee), per the Wikipedia summary retrieved for "Alabama."
- **Population during period:** `place_population` could not return data for "Mississippi Territory, United States" — this is a tool coverage gap, not evidence of no population; report it as unconfirmed rather than stating a figure.
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by the tools used in this survey.
- **Ethnic composition:** The Creek and Cherokee nations inhabited much of the territory, with growing Anglo-American settlement from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia, intensifying after the Creek War of 1813–1814 (Wikipedia).
- **Religious denominations:** Not confirmed by the tools used in this survey.
- **Key historical events:** Early European presence centered on Mobile Bay (French settlement, 1702); later contested among France, Britain, and Spain before U.S. territorial organization; the Creek War (1813–1814) reshaped settlement patterns just after the period of interest (Wikipedia).

## Boundary changes
- The region had no stable American civil jurisdiction in 1800: it was part of Mississippi Territory (1798–1817) per `place_search`, itself carved from land Georgia and Spain had claimed, and it was reorganized as Alabama Territory in 1817 before statehood in 1819 (Wikipedia). A researcher following a family through this period must treat the Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory as one continuous administrative trail — records for the same family and the same physical location may be filed under either territorial name depending on the exact year.
- The Gulf Coast strip around Mobile remained under Spanish administration as part of West Florida into the early 1810s; records for that area before U.S. annexation may be Spanish colonial records, not American territorial ones.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No FamilySearch Wiki page returned jurisdiction-specific registration dates for this territory; every `wiki_place_page` call for "Mississippi Territory, United States" (home, research_tips, online_records, getting_started) came back as the generic fallback "Genealogy Research Guide" template rather than place-specific content, so no date can be cited.
- **What exists:** There was no statewide civil vital registration in this territorial period; expect no birth/marriage/death registers at a territorial level.
- **Where held:** N/A — not confirmed.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers and county marriage bonds (see Church records and Probate/court below) are the substitute sources for this era.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Not confirmed by any tool in this survey — no page returned specific congregation or denomination data for this place/period.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials would be the expected content, per the generic FamilySearch Wiki "Genealogy Records" template read at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Genealogy_Records, but that page is generic guidance, not a Mississippi Territory-specific source.
- **Where held:** `collections_search` (scope "Mississippi") did return a real, place-relevant hit: **"Mississippi, Church Records, 1800-1950"** (collection id 2034891, 87,654 persons), whose date range opens exactly at 1800 — directly useful for this period. Build its link from `https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891`.
- **Gaps:** Specific denominational survival/loss could not be confirmed.
- **Language:** English expected; not separately confirmed.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** No 1800 or 1810 federal census page data was returned specific to this territory by the tools used; nationally, decennial federal census began in 1790 per the generic wiki template, but Mississippi Territory-specific survival is not confirmed here.
- **State/provincial census:** `collections_search` returned **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890"** (id 1927171, 198,340 persons) — its range (1792 on) covers the Mississippi Territory period and is the relevant census-substitute collection, important because the 1800/1810 federal Alabama-area returns are largely lost and such compiled substitutes (tax lists, muster rolls) typically stand in for them.

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships — per generic wiki guidance, filed at the county/district level.

- **Testate or intestate:** Not determinable without a specific person.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey applied once U.S. land offices opened in the territory (not independently confirmed here).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** `collections_search` returned **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907"** (id 1919694, 312,450 persons) — its start year (1798) matches the Mississippi Territory's creation and is the key land-grant/patent source for this period.

Based on general U.S. research practice the Mississippi Department of Archives and History and the Alabama Department of Archives and History are the conventional candidates for surviving territorial-era papers, but this was not confirmed by any tool result here, so it is not asserted as fact.

## Records NOT online
Specific territorial vital records, tax lists, and militia muster rolls for 1798–1819 were not found as separate online collections or digitized browsable volumes in this survey (`volume_search` and `catalog_search` both came back empty). Treat these as likely paper-only or undigitized, not as nonexistent.

No tool result in this survey confirmed a specific record loss (e.g., a courthouse fire) for this territory — this cannot be stated as fact and is not asserted.

- Direct answer to your browsable-volumes question: **none were found.** `volume_search` scoped to "Mississippi Territory, United States" for 1798–1819 returned `totalResults: 0` with no volumes of any kind (indexed, browse-only, or full-text) — there is currently no digitized, image-browsable volume set for this specific territory/period in FamilySearch's volume index.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced, now saved as **loc_001** in your project's `research.json`:

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860s–1890s)

**Coverage:** Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (the core anthracite county; a representative survey)

### Key Records & Where They're Held

| Record Type | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Church registers (Catholic & Protestant) | 1840s–1900s | Digitized on FamilySearch — browse only (not name-indexed), film by film |
| Marriage registers | 1860s–1890s | County courthouse & diocese archives; partially digitized |
| Naturalization records | 1860s–1890s | Schuylkill County courthouse; browse-only on FamilySearch |
| Probate/orphans' court | 1860s–1890s | County courthouse; browse-only |
| Deed books | 1800s–1900s | Partially name-indexed on FamilySearch |
| **Coal-company payroll index** | ~1860s–1900s | Specialized index on FamilySearch — ~41,000 mineworkers with job, wages, and home parish |

### Jurisdictional Notes for Irish Catholic Research

- **Diocese boundary split (1868):** Schuylkill County Catholic parishes remained under the **Philadelphia Archdiocese** throughout this period. Neighboring coal counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna) transferred to the newly created **Scranton Diocese** in 1868. Using the wrong diocesan archives is a common pitfall.
- **State vital registration:** Pennsylvania's official civil birth/marriage/death registration began in 1906. For the 1860s–1890s, **church registers are your primary vital record source**.
- County-level civil death returns exist in some townships from the 1850s–1870s but are very incomplete.

### The Coal-Region Payroll Index (High Priority for Irish Miners)
The most specialized resource: a FamilySearch index built from coal-company payroll records listing roughly **41,000 mineworkers** in Schuylkill County. Fields include job title, wages, and importantly — **home parish** — which can directly point you to the Irish county of origin or the local parish for church register searches.

### Other Coal Counties (Separate Surveys Needed)
This guide covers Schuylkill County. The other anthracite counties each have their own record landscape and would each need their own locality survey:
- **Luzerne County** (Wilkes-Barre area)
- **Lackawanna County** (Scranton, carved from Luzerne in 1878)
- **Carbon County** (Mauch Chunk / Jim Thorpe area)
- **Northumberland County** (Shamokin area)

### Recommended Starting Points for Irish Ancestors
1. Search the **coal-company payroll index** first — the home-parish field is invaluable.
2. Identify the specific township/borough to target the right **Catholic parish register**.
3. Check Philadelphia Archdiocesan Archives for Schuylkill County parishes; Scranton Diocesan Archives for Luzerne/Lackawanna parishes.
4. Naturalization records (1860s–1880s) often name the county of origin in Ireland.
5. 1880 US Census is fully indexed and gives birthplaces for both parents.

---

# Locality Guide: Vermont, United States (pre-statehood, c. 1770–1791)

## Jurisdiction Overview
Vermont was not its own recognized jurisdiction until 1791. Before 1777 the territory was disputed between the Province of New Hampshire (which issued "New Hampshire Grants" to townships from the 1740s–1760s) and the Province of New York, which refused to recognize those grants. The territory declared itself the independent **Vermont Republic** in 1777 and operated as an unrecognized republic until admitted as the 14th U.S. state in 1791. County-level governance within the republic only began after 1777; before that, administration ran through town proprietors and the competing colonial authorities.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Vermont Genealogy," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)*

---

## Boundary & Jurisdiction Cautions
Because the territory was contested by **both New Hampshire and New York** before 1777, records for the same towns and families may be filed under either colony's record series — not under a "Vermont" heading at all. Researchers should search New Hampshire and New York colonial record series in parallel with any Vermont-labeled collections.

---

## Available Record Types

### Land Records ⭐ (Most Important for This Period)
- **1771 New York Grant Survey Schedule** — The earliest systematic resident list for the future state. Prepared under New York colonial authority, it enumerates roughly 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize, with grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This is the closest thing to a census for 1770s Vermont.
- **Township/proprietors' records** — New England-style town grants, originally issued by New Hampshire; competing New York grants also exist.
- **Town histories (secondary source)** — 19th-century Vermont town histories (mostly published 1860–1900) often **reprint colonial-era proprietors' records** that are otherwise difficult to access and are an important substitute for lost or inaccessible originals.

### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1857** — far after the target period.
- Some town clerk records survive "back to the 1770s," but survival is **uneven and town-by-town** — there is no central pre-1857 index.
- **Where held:** Individual town clerk offices; no statewide index exists.
- **Alternative:** Church registers (not confirmed for specific denominations by this survey) and land/proprietors' records.

### Census Records
- The first federal census was 1790 (Vermont's associated enumeration is 1791, the year of statehood).
- **No pre-statehood state or provincial census was confirmed** by this survey's tools.
- The **1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (see Land Records above) is the best pre-census substitute.

### Military Records
- The **American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)** falls squarely in this period.
- Vermont raised its own militia ("Green Mountain Boys") independent of Continental Congress authorization in parts of this era.
- Record types: service records, pension files, bounty land warrants.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA), https://www.archives.gov/

### Probate & Court Records
- Likely held at county courthouses once Vermont organized counties after 1777.
- No Vermont-specific pre-statehood probate collection was confirmed by this survey's tools.

### Church Records
- Not confirmed for specific denominations or repositories for 1770–1791 Vermont by this survey.
- Given Vermont's New Hampshire/Massachusetts settler origins, Congregationalist and similar New England churches are plausible — but no specific register series was confirmed.

### Cemetery Records
- Not confirmed for this period in this survey. Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a general resource.

### Newspaper Records
- Printing in the territory during this era was minimal; no Vermont pre-statehood newspaper titles were confirmed by this survey.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont town clerk offices | Town vital records "some back to the 1770s," uneven survival | In-person or mail to specific town |
| County courthouses (post-1777 VT counties) | Land, probate, court records | In-person / mail |
| NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) | Revolutionary War service, pension, bounty land records | Free |
| FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/) | General search; no Vermont 1770–1791 indexed collections confirmed by this survey | Free |
| Ancestry (https://www.ancestry.com/) | General census and record collections | Subscription |
| Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) | Cemetery records | Free |

---

## Online Coverage Gap — Important Warning
This survey's collection, volume, and catalog searches on FamilySearch returned **zero indexed collections** for Vermont in 1770–1791. This means most pre-statehood Vermont records are **not yet confirmed online** — they are likely on paper only in town clerk offices, county archives, or reprinted in 19th-century town histories. This is a digitization gap, not evidence the records do not exist.

---

## Known Record Losses
No specific Vermont pre-statehood record set was confirmed as destroyed by this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki describes only *uneven survival* of town vital records — a gap in coverage, not confirmed destruction.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — it predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state.
2. **Search New Hampshire AND New York colonial records** for the same towns and families — before 1777 your ancestors' records may be filed under either colony, not under "Vermont."
3. **Go directly to town clerks** for pre-1857 vital records; do not expect a statewide index.
4. **Consult 19th-century Vermont town histories** (1860–1900) as a secondary source reprinting otherwise-inaccessible colonial-era proprietors' records.
5. **Check Revolutionary War records at NARA** for any male ancestors in the 1775–1783 period — service, pension, and bounty land records can fill gaps left by missing vital records.
6. Online tools turned up nothing for this early period — plan to contact Vermont's State Archives and individual town clerks directly rather than relying on indexed databases.

The guide for Yorkshire, England (1851) is complete and saved as **loc_001**. Here's what the locality-guide agent found:

---

## Yorkshire, England — Death Records, 1851

### Civil Registration (Primary Source)
- **England and Wales Death Registration Index** — Civil death registration began nationwide in **1837**, so a Yorkshire death in 1851 is fully within the civil registration era.
- Deaths were recorded quarterly at the **General Register Office (GRO)**. The GRO index is searchable free at:
  - **FreeBMD** (freebmd.org.uk)
  - **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org)
  - **Ancestry** (ancestry.co.uk)
- The full death certificate (with cause of death, informant, and address) must be ordered separately from the **GRO**.

### Church Burial Registers
- Church of England parish burial registers run parallel to civil registration and can confirm place and date of burial, often with more local detail.

### Supporting Records
- **1851 Census** — Taken in March 1851, this can place your ancestor in a household and confirm their county and address. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Local Newspapers** — Yorkshire newspapers from 1851 may carry death notices.
- **YorkshireBMD** (yorkshirebmd.org.uk) — A free county-specific index with transcriptions of births, marriages, and deaths.

### ⚠️ Important — Yorkshire's Sub-Divisions
Yorkshire is divided into three historic **Ridings** (administrative sub-regions):
- **West Riding**
- **North Riding**
- **East Riding**

Records are often filed by Riding rather than under "Yorkshire" as a whole. Run your searches against each riding by name for the best results.

---

**Suggested next step:** Use the **research-plan** agent to build a concrete, staged search plan for your ancestor's death record. If you share the person's name, I can help direct that.

I built a locality guide for Yorkshire, England, covering records around the year 1851 for a death record search. Civil deaths in England and Wales were recorded nationally by the General Register Office starting in 1837, so a Yorkshire death in 1851 should appear in the England and Wales Death Registration Index, searchable free through FreeBMD or FamilySearch, with the full certificate ordered separately from the GRO; alongside that, Church of England parish burial registers and the 1851 census (also found through FamilySearch and Ancestry) can confirm the person's location and household, and local newspapers from that year, plus county-specific free indexes like YorkshireBMD, offer additional corroboration. One important wrinkle: Yorkshire's records are often filed by its historic sub-regions (West, North, East Riding) rather than under "Yorkshire" as a whole, so searches should be run against each riding by name, and some FamilySearch Wiki background pages could not be retrieved with place-specific detail this time, so registration start-date details should be double-checked directly on the wiki before being relied on.

# Locality Guide: Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom (1851)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Yorkshire is a historic county recorded by `place_search` as existing from circa 866 (date range "+866/+1801"), re-standardized under "Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom" from 1801 onward.
- **County seat / administrative center:** No single seat — Yorkshire was historically divided into three Ridings (North, East, West) plus the city of York; record collections are filed under those riding names (see Boundary changes).
- **Parent jurisdiction:** England, United Kingdom.
- **Population during period:** `place_population` could not return figures for "Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom" for 1841–1861 in this survey — not confirmed; not a reported absence of population, just a tool gap this run.
- **Economy:** Not confirmed by any tool result in this survey (no FamilySearch Wiki page returned Yorkshire-specific content).
- **Ethnic composition:** Not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.
- **Religious denominations:** `collections_search` shows substantial Church of England parish-register holdings for Yorkshire plus separately catalogued Non-Conformist collections for West Yorkshire, indicating both established church and nonconformist congregations were present; no further denominational detail was confirmed.
- **Key historical events:** Not confirmed by any tool result in this survey.

## Boundary changes
- Yorkshire appears in `place_search_all`-type lookup as two successive standard-place records: "Yorkshire, England" (+866/+1801) and "Yorkshire, England, United Kingdom" (+1801/present) — a naming/jurisdiction-label change around 1801, not a territorial split.
- Separately, record collections treat Yorkshire as split into the three historic Ridings (West Riding, North Riding, East Riding) plus York itself — this is not a change during 1851 but the standing administrative/record-keeping structure, so any search must check collections filed under "West Yorkshire", "North Yorkshire", "East Riding", and "York" individually as well as "Yorkshire" generally.
- No boundary change specific to 1851 was confirmed by any tool result in this survey.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Civil registration of deaths in England and Wales is a national (statewide-equivalent) system. The FamilySearch Wiki's England Vital Records page could not be read with jurisdiction-specific content in this survey (it returned only generic placeholder text) — the commonly cited 1 July 1837 start could not be confirmed from a tool result this run and should be re-checked.
- **What exists:** `collections_search` returned "England and Wales, Death Registration Index 1837-2007" (id 2285341, 87,352,096 people) — this is the GRO civil death index covering 1851.
- **Where held:** General Register Office (national level); indexed copy searchable via FamilySearch collection 2285341 and, per `external_links_search`, also at FreeBMD (https://www.freebmd.org.uk/search) and findmypast's "England & Wales Deaths, 1837-2007" filtered to Yorkshire.
- **Gaps:** The GRO index gives name/quarter/district/volume-page only, not cause of death or full detail — the full certificate must be ordered separately from the GRO.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church of England burial registers (see Church records) predate and run alongside civil registration.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Church of England (established); Non-Conformist congregations also had records kept separately for West Yorkshire — per `collections_search` and `external_links_search` results below. No founding dates were confirmed by any tool result.
- **Record types:** `collections_search` returned "England, Yorkshire, Parish Registers, 1538-2016" (id 4439317, 27,344,590 people, covering 1851) and "England, Yorkshire, Bishop's Transcripts, 1547-1957" (id 4319956, 11,853,270 people, covering 1851) — both include burials.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch (above IDs); `external_links_search` also lists "West Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials, 1813-1985" (ancestry.com/search/collections/2254) and "North Yorkshire, England, Church of England Deaths and Burials, 1813-1995" (ancestry.com/search/collections/62238) on Ancestry; findmypast's "Yorkshire Burials" (http://search.findmypast.co.uk/search-world-Records/yorkshire-burials) and "Yorkshire Parish Registers and Bishop's Transcripts" (browse).
- **Gaps:** No tool result in this survey identified a specific denomination or year span with no surviving registers for 1851 — not confirmed either way.
- **Language:** English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** `collections_search` confirms "England and Wales, Census, 1851" (id 2563939, 1,569,726 people) — the census closest to the target year; also 1841 and 1861 censuses are listed, useful to bracket a death between enumerations.
- **State/provincial census:** Not applicable (no sub-national census system confirmed).

- **Access:** The 1851 census collection (id 2563939) is listed by `collections_search` as a named FamilySearch collection; indexing level (name-indexed vs. browse-only) was not detailed in the tool's response — treat as likely indexed given it is a named person-count collection, but confirm on the collection page itself.

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, and death duty records. `collections_search` lists "Yorkshire, England, Probate Records, 1521-1858" on Ancestry (collections/5246) and "England and Wales, Index to Death Duty Registers, 1796-1903" (FamilySearch id 4114269, 3,377,366 people, covers 1851).
- **Testate or intestate:** Not known for this case — search both a will (testate) and an administration (intestate) series, since which applies is not yet established.
- **Date range:** 1521-1858 for the Yorkshire probate collection, which covers 1851; before 1858 English probate was handled by ecclesiastical courts (Prerogative Court of Canterbury or diocesan/peculiar courts), not a unified civil probate registry.
